title: Animals without backbones: how they breathe with no lungs

summary.text: An ant has no lungs, an earthworm has no nose and a crab keeps her gills under her shell. Yet every one of them takes in oxygen all day long. In a jelly cube, colour creeps in only a few millimetres, and oxygen drifts through a body in that same slow way. So a thick body needs help: skin that stays thin and wet, gills that water is pushed over, air tubes that reach every part, or lungs. This unit follows the air into worms, ants, crabs, snails and spiders, and finds out why one slow drift shapes so many different bodies.
summary.art: A cutaway of an ant, an earthworm and a crab side by side, with thin lines showing air reaching each body in a different way.

intro.hook: Take a deep breath and feel your chest rise. Now think of an ant. An ant has no lungs and no chest. A crab has no nose. An earthworm has neither. All three breathe all day long. How?
intro.text: Here is a clue. Your body is made of billions of tiny cells, and every cell needs oxygen all the time. In you, blood carries the oxygen round. But an ant's blood does not carry most of her oxygen, and a worm has no lungs at all. In this unit you will watch how slowly colour creeps into jelly. Then you will see why that one slow drift shapes a worm, an ant, a crab and a spider into such different animals.
intro.art: A child with a magnifying glass looking at an ant on a table, with a thought bubble that shows a tiny lung with a question mark.

outcomes: I can explain that colour and oxygen drift slowly, and that going twice as far takes about four times as long.
I can show, with squares or cubes, that a bigger body has more inside for each bit of outside.
I can name four ways that animals without backbones get oxygen: through the skin, with gills, with air tubes, and with book lungs or a lung sac.
I can explain why a thin worm can breathe through skin alone, but a thick animal needs gills, tubes or lungs.
I can say why water holds much less oxygen than air, and why warm, still water can run short of it.
I can say how open blood differs from closed blood, and that an insect's blood does not carry most of the oxygen.
I can run a fair test, fill in a table, and say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can name two questions about these animals that scientists still argue about.

terms.meaning: A gas in air and water that almost every animal needs. Cells use it to get energy from food.
terms.art: A flask of air with one fifth of the little dots coloured blue to show oxygen.

terms.meaning: Taking oxygen into a body and letting carbon dioxide out, across a thin, wet surface.
terms.example: An earthworm does gas exchange all over their skin.
terms.art: An arrow of oxygen going into a thin skin and an arrow of carbon dioxide going out.

terms.meaning: The slow spreading of tiny particles from where there are many to where there are few. Nothing pushes them. They simply wander.
terms.example: A drop of food colour in still jelly spreads out by diffusion.
terms.art: A drop of red colour in a glass of clear jelly spreading outward in a soft cloud.

terms.meaning: The size of all the outside of something, counting every face and fold.
terms.example: A feathery gill has far more surface area than a smooth lump of the same size.
terms.art: A smooth block next to a block cut into thin slices, with the outside faces shaded.

terms.meaning: Oxygen that is mixed into water as invisible particles, which gills can take in.
terms.example: A warm, still pond has less dissolved oxygen than a cool, moving stream.
terms.art: A glass of water with tiny blue dots spread through it.

terms.meaning: A thin, feathery body part that takes dissolved oxygen out of water.
terms.example: A mud crab has gills in a chamber under her shell.
terms.art: A crab with the side of her shell lifted to show rows of feathery gills.

terms.meaning: One of the tiny holes along the sides of an insect, where air goes in and out.
terms.example: A caterpillar has a row of spiracles down each side.
terms.art: A caterpillar seen from the side with a row of small dark dots along its body.

terms.meaning: A thin air tube inside an insect or spider. The plural is tracheae. Tracheae branch into finer and finer tubes that reach every part.
terms.example: An ant's tracheae carry air straight to her muscles.
terms.art: An ant cut open to show white branching tubes running from the side holes to the legs.

terms.meaning: A stack of thin plates, like the pages of a book, inside a spider or scorpion. Air flows between the plates and blood flows through them.
terms.example: A house spider has book lungs under her belly.
terms.art: A spider's belly with a small slit opening onto a stack of thin pages.

terms.meaning: The blood-like liquid of insects, crabs, snails and spiders. It carries food and messages round the body. In an insect, the haemolymph does not carry most of the oxygen.
terms.example: The clear green liquid in a squashed grasshopper is haemolymph.
terms.art: A cutaway grasshopper with pale green liquid around the organs.

terms.meaning: A body plan where the blood-like liquid leaves the vessels and soaks all round the organs.
terms.example: Crabs, insects and snails have open circulation.
terms.art: A heart pouring pale liquid out into a body space, where organs sit in it.

terms.meaning: A body plan where the blood stays inside tubes all the way round.
terms.example: People and earthworms have closed circulation.
terms.art: A loop of red tubes with a heart in the middle, and no liquid outside the tubes.

explanations.concept: Oxygen drifts slowly, and the time grows faster than the distance
explanations.definition: Diffusion is the spreading of particles by their own random movement. The time it takes to spread across a distance grows with the square of the distance: twice as far takes about four times as long.
explanations.description: Every particle of colour or oxygen jiggles and bumps about at random. Some wander in, some wander out, and slowly the particles spread. Over a tiny distance this is quick. Over a long distance it is very slow, because each step forward can be undone by a step back. In your Colour Cubes, the colour crept in about the same few millimetres whether the cube was small or big. Oxygen moves through water and through flesh in this same way. In water, it drifts about ten thousand times more slowly than in air. So an animal whose middle is a long way from the outside cannot rely on drifting alone.
explanations.context: In Colour Cubes and the Wobbly Walk game, you saw that things spread slowly over distance. This card says why.
examples: A drop of food colour in still jelly reaches about 2 millimetres in half an hour, but 2 centimetres is 10 times as far, so it would take about 100 times as long. That is days.
Oxygen drifting in from an earthworm's skin reaches a cell 1 millimetre inside quickly, but a cell 1 centimetre inside much too slowly.
The smell of a cooking tadka reaches the next room quickly only because moving air carries it. In still air it would take far longer.
explanations.art: A row of coloured dots that start on the left and spread to the right, with a small distance marked 1 and a double distance marked 4.

explanations.concept: Bigger bodies have less outside for the inside they hold
explanations.definition: As a body gets bigger, its inside grows faster than its outside. A cube twice as wide has four times the outside and eight times the inside.
explanations.description: Look at a cube 1 centimetre wide. It has 6 square centimetres of outside and 1 cubic centimetre of inside. Now make a cube 2 centimetres wide. The outside grows to 24 square centimetres, which is 4 times more. But the inside grows to 8 cubic centimetres, which is 8 times more. Each bit of inside has only half as much outside to reach. This is why a tiny animal can breathe through their skin, and a big one cannot. As a body grows, it must find new ways to bring the outside nearer: a thin shape, folds, tubes or a pump.
explanations.context: You counted squares in Ring or Core and measured white centres in Colour Cubes. This card puts the two ideas together.
examples: A flatworm is thin as a leaf, so every cell is close to the outside.
A crab is thick, so she folds her outside into gills.
A baby elephant and a mouse breathe the same air, but only the elephant needs big lungs folded into her chest.
explanations.art: A 1 centimetre cube and a 2 centimetre cube side by side, with the number of outside faces and the amount of inside written on each.

explanations.concept: Skin breathing: thin, wet and everywhere
explanations.definition: Skin breathing is gas exchange through the whole outer surface. It works only for bodies that are thin or small, and only while the skin stays wet.
explanations.description: Oxygen can only enter a body when it is dissolved in water. So an earthworm keeps a thin film of wet slime on her skin. Air dissolves into the slime, drifts through the thin skin, and meets her blood. Under the skin, tiny blood vessels run close to the surface. The oxygen is picked up by red haemoglobin dissolved in her blood, and carried round by five pairs of muscular tubes that work like hearts. A dry earthworm cannot breathe, which is why worms die on hot, dry pavements. Flatworms, jellyfish and many other thin animals breathe through their skin in the same way.
explanations.context: An earthworm has no lungs and no gills. This card explains how she still gets enough air.
examples: An earthworm in damp soil breathes through her wet skin.
A flatworm in a pond takes oxygen in through the whole body, and has no separate lungs or gills.
A jellyfish is almost all water, with only thin layers of living cells, so oxygen reaches every cell.
explanations.art: A cross-section of an earthworm's skin with a wet film on top, oxygen dots drifting in, and a small blood vessel just below.

explanations.concept: Gills: moving water over a feathery surface
explanations.definition: A gill is a thin, folded body part that takes dissolved oxygen out of water and lets carbon dioxide out.
explanations.description: Water holds about thirty times less oxygen than the same amount of air, and warm water holds even less. So an animal with gills must pass a lot of water over them. A mud crab keeps her gills in chambers under the sides of her shell. A flap near her mouth, called a gill bailer, beats back and forth and draws water through. The gills are feathery, so their surface is large. Thin walls let oxygen drift in to the blood in a very short distance. Prawns, mussels, octopuses and the young of dragonflies breathe with gills too. If the water stands still, the water next to the gills runs short of oxygen. The crab can only fix that by moving the water, or by moving to better water.
explanations.context: In the story, a crab climbed to the top of his box before dawn. This card explains why.
examples: A mud crab has gills under her shell and a gill bailer that pumps water over them.
A mussel draws water through her body all day, to breathe and to feed.
A young dragonfly in a pond has gills inside her tail end and squirts water in and out.
explanations.art: A mud crab with the side of her shell lifted, showing feathery gills, with arrows for water flowing in at her legs and out near her mouth.

explanations.concept: Air tubes: the insect's way of reaching every cell
explanations.definition: Insects breathe through spiracles, small holes along their sides, which lead into tracheae, air tubes that branch until they touch almost every cell.
explanations.description: An insect does not breathe in at one place and send the oxygen round in blood. Instead, air goes in through the spiracles and along the tracheae. The tubes branch again and again, down to threads thinner than a hair. The finest ones end right against the cells that need the oxygen. Oxygen drifts about ten thousand times faster through air than through water. So drifting along a tube is fast enough for a small body. Larger insects also pump their bellies to push air along. Most insects can close their spiracles to save water. Because the air goes straight to the cells, an insect's blood does not need to carry most of the oxygen.
explanations.context: An ant has no lungs, yet she runs fast and lifts crumbs bigger than her head. This card shows how.
examples: An ant has a row of tiny holes down each side of her body.
A caterpillar has a row of dark dots along her sides, which are her spiracles.
A diving beetle carries a bubble of air under her wing covers, and her air tubes open into it.
explanations.art: An ant cut open to show white tubes branching from small side holes to the head, legs and tummy.

explanations.definition: A book lung is a stack of thin plates inside a spider or scorpion, with air between the plates and blood flowing through them. A land snail has a lung sac, a pocket lined with blood vessels.
explanations.description: Land animals have a problem that water animals do not. A wet breathing surface dries out in air. The answer is to hide the surface inside the body, in a pocket that has only a small opening. A spider folds hers into a stack of thin plates, which gives a huge surface in a tiny space. Many spiders also have air tubes. A land snail has a pocket under her shell with a small opening called a breathing pore. She opens and closes it as she needs. Some pond snails have lungs too, and swim up to the surface for air. The coconut crab of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands has gills that have changed into a lung-like organ, so she breathes air and drowns in deep water.
explanations.context: Animals that live on land cannot keep a wet skin on the outside. This card shows how they keep their breathing surface wet and safe.
examples: A house spider has book lungs under her belly.
A garden snail opens a breathing pore on the right side of her body.
A coconut crab breathes air, though her cousins in the sea breathe water.
explanations.art: A spider's belly cut open to show two stacks of thin plates like pages of a book.

explanations.definition: In closed circulation, blood stays inside tubes. In open circulation, a blood-like liquid called haemolymph leaves the tubes and soaks all round the organs.
explanations.description: People, earthworms and octopuses have closed circulation. Crabs, insects, spiders and most snails have open circulation. In an open system, a simple heart pumps the haemolymph out into the body space. It soaks round the organs, then drifts back to the heart through small openings. This is slower and uses less pressure, but it works well in a small body. In an insect, the haemolymph carries food, waste and the cells that fight germs, but most of the oxygen goes straight down the air tubes. In a crab or a spider, the haemolymph does carry oxygen, using a blue copper-based substance, so it turns blue when it meets the air. Our own red blood uses iron instead.
explanations.context: Your blood carries oxygen round your body. This card shows that other animals do it differently, or not at all.
examples: A grasshopper's heart is a long tube along her back, and her haemolymph soaks round her organs.
A crab's haemolymph turns pale blue when it meets oxygen.
An earthworm's red blood stays inside tubes all the way round.
explanations.art: Two diagrams side by side: red liquid running in closed loops in an earthworm, and pale liquid soaking round the organs of a grasshopper.

explanations.concept: Why there are no giant insects today
explanations.description: About 300 million years ago, dragonfly-like insects had wings up to about 70 centimetres across. Today the largest insects are far smaller. Scientists agree that an insect's air tubes work best in a small body. They do not agree on what limited the size of the giants, or why they disappeared.
explanations.context: You saw that tubes work well for small bodies. This card asks whether tubes set a limit on how big an insect can be.
examples: Meganeura, an extinct giant dragonfly relative, had wings about 65 to 70 centimetres across.
Today's biggest insects, such as the goliath beetle of Africa, are about as long as a child's hand.
explanations.art: A giant dragonfly the size of a crow flying beside a child's hand for scale.

perspectives.explanation: Air once held more oxygen, perhaps about a third instead of a fifth, and more oxygen can drift further along a tube. In experiments, fruit flies raised in air with more oxygen grew a little bigger over several generations.
Later, flying birds and flying reptiles began to hunt big insects. Small, quick insects survived better, so the giants may have been eaten rather than starved of air.
Insects must shed their hard outer skin to grow. A very big insect would be very heavy while soft and weak. Tubes, weight and moulting may all limit size together.

explanations.concept: Why earthworms come up when it rains
explanations.description: After heavy rain, earthworms appear on roads and paths. Almost everyone has seen it. Nobody has settled why it happens.
explanations.context: Earthworms breathe through their skin, so people often guess that rain makes them come up for air. This card gives the main ideas.
examples: Earthworms on a wet road after the first monsoon showers.
Worms crawling up the wall of a flowerpot after heavy watering.
explanations.art: A wet road after rain with several earthworms crawling across it and raindrops falling.

perspectives.explanation: Water fills the soil and the air in the burrow runs short. The worms come up to breathe. A problem with this idea is that worms can live under well-aired water for days.
Wet ground is the one time worms can cross open ground without drying out. So rain is their chance to move to new soil.
The patter of rain may feel like a mole digging, and moles eat worms. Some worms are known to leave the soil when it shakes, so rain may feel like danger.

explanations.concept: Where the oxygen comes from, and where it goes
explanations.definition: Oxygen in air and water is made mostly by plants, algae and tiny bacteria using sunlight. Animals use it inside their cells to release energy from food.
explanations.description: Inside each cell are tiny parts called mitochondria. They use oxygen to release the energy stored in food, a little like a very slow, gentle burning. The waste gas is carbon dioxide. Every breath of every animal is part of this. The oxygen itself was made by plants and by tiny living beings in the sea. About 2.4 billion years ago, tiny bacteria in the sea began to make so much oxygen that the air changed. Animals came much later, and they have been using that gift ever since. Nothing the ant, the crab or the worm breathes was made by an animal.
explanations.context: We followed oxygen from the air into the body. This card follows it one step further, to the cell, and one step back, to its source.
examples: A mud crab uses oxygen in her muscle cells to power her claws.
Green pond weed makes oxygen in daylight, and uses some of it up at night.
The oxygen in a village pond in the morning was made by pond plants and algae the day before.
explanations.art: A green plant in sunlight on the left, a crab under water on the right, and blue dots drifting from the plant to the crab.

agreed.text: Animals take in oxygen across a thin, wet surface and let carbon dioxide out the same way.
agreed.evidence: Oxygen sensors in sealed jars show the oxygen falling and carbon dioxide rising when worms, snails, crabs or insects are inside.

agreed.text: Earthworms breathe mainly through their skin, and need it to stay damp.
agreed.evidence: Earthworms have no lungs or gills when opened up, and they stop moving when their skin dries.

agreed.text: Insects breathe through spiracles and tracheae, and most insects' blood does not carry most of the oxygen.
agreed.evidence: Marcello Malpighi saw the spiracles and air tubes of a silkworm in 1669. In 2003, X-ray pictures of living beetles, crickets and ants showed the big air tubes in the head and chest squeezing and widening again.

agreed.text: Water holds far less oxygen than air, and warm water holds less than cold water.
agreed.evidence: Dissolved oxygen meters give about 7 to 9 milligrams in a litre of water at 20 to 30 degrees. A litre of air holds about 280 milligrams of oxygen.

agreed.text: Spiders and scorpions have book lungs, and land snails have a lung sac.
agreed.evidence: Opening these animals up shows the stacked plates and the blood-vessel-lined pocket.

agreed.text: The time for particles to drift across a distance grows with the square of the distance.
agreed.evidence: Albert Einstein worked it out in 1905. Jean Perrin's careful measurements of tiny particles in water confirmed it a few years later.

challenging.claim: Only animals with lungs really breathe.
challenging.for: People have lungs, and a chest that rises and falls is easy to see.
challenging.against: Every animal needs oxygen for every cell. Worms, crabs and ants breathe too, with skin, gills and tubes. A lung is one way to do the job, not the only way.

challenging.claim: Animals without red blood are bloodless and breathe less.
challenging.who: Aristotle, an ancient Greek thinker, called animals such as insects 'bloodless'.
challenging.for: An insect has no red blood, and her body is mostly tubes and soft parts.
challenging.against: Insects have haemolymph, and their air tubes carry oxygen straight to their cells. An ant uses oxygen at a high rate for her size. Red blood is one way to carry oxygen, not the only one.

challenging.for: An ant is tiny and has far fewer cells than a mouse.
challenging.against: An ant has tubes that reach every cell, muscles, eyes, and a nest of thousands. Being small does not make a body or a mind simple.

challenging.claim: Earthworms come up in the rain because they would otherwise drown.
challenging.for: Flooded soil can run short of oxygen, and worms breathe through their skin.
challenging.against: Worms can survive in well-aired water for days. Some also come up in light rain when the soil is not flooded.

challenging.claim: Giant insects vanished because the air lost oxygen.
challenging.for: The giant insects lived when oxygen was higher. Fruit flies raised in more oxygen grew bigger over several generations.
challenging.against: Other scientists point to flying hunters that appeared later, and to the weight of a giant body. The fossil record has gaps, so the cause is still uncertain.

challenging.claim: A crab drowns if she leaves the water, so crabs are water animals only.
challenging.for: Most crabs have gills and must keep them wet.
challenging.against: The coconut crab of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands has a lung-like organ. She breathes air, climbs coconut palms, and would drown if kept under water.

big_questions.q: The colour crept only a few millimetres into a big jelly cube. What would a worm as thick as a tree trunk have to do to stay alive?
big_questions.hint: Think about tubes, folds and pumps, and which ones the animals in this unit already use.

big_questions.q: Your blood carries oxygen to your cells. An ant's blood does not. How can an ant be so fast and strong?
big_questions.hint: Where does an ant's oxygen travel, and how far must the oxygen go?

big_questions.q: Water holds about 30 times less oxygen than air, yet animals began in water. What does that tell you about the first animals?
big_questions.hint: Think about how thick and how active a body can be when air is scarce.

big_questions.q: A coconut crab drowns in the sea but is still a crab. Is breathing air or water a feature of the animal, or of where she lives?
big_questions.hint: Think of a pond snail that has a lung but lives in water.

big_questions.q: The oxygen you breathe was made by plants and tiny sea microbes. Whose air is it?
big_questions.hint: Follow one breath of air backward, as far as you can.

big_questions.q: You breathe in through your nose and an ant takes air in through holes in her sides. Are you both doing the same thing, or two different things with one name?
big_questions.hint: What does each body need to happen, and what is different about how it happens?

big_questions.q: Libbie Hyman wrote a six-volume book on animals without backbones, by herself, over about 27 years. Why might someone give their life to animals most people step over?
big_questions.hint: Think about who gets noticed in science, and who does not.

big_questions.q: Is a bigger body better? What can a big body do that a small one cannot, and the other way round?
big_questions.hint: Think about strength, speed, hiding, breathing and eating.

big_questions.q: Each kind of animal has a different way of getting air. Is there one right way to breathe?
big_questions.hint: Right for a mud crab, a spider and a human might not be the same.

story.title: The Crabs That Rose at Dawn
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. Mud crabs are fattened in boxes in the backwaters of Kerala, and tidal gates let the tide in. The air dissolved in a pond is lowest just before dawn, because plants and animals use it up through the night. Anjana, Ammamma and Miss Radha are imagined.
text: Anjana lived with her grandmother, Ammamma, on Vypin Island near Kochi. Behind their house lay a pond of salty backwater, joined to the wide backwater by a wooden gate. In the pond floated twenty-four plastic boxes. In each box sat one mud crab, who was being fattened for the market.

Mud crabs fight if you keep them together, so every crab had a box of her own. Every evening Ammamma fed them chopped fish. In three weeks each crab would be heavy and ready to sell. The money paid for Anjana's school books.

In April the nights turned hot and still. On Monday morning Ammamma found two crabs floating on their backs. On Tuesday she found four. 'Bad luck,' said Ammamma. She tied a red thread round the post, because that was what her own mother used to do.
Anjana did not think it was luck. Luck did not come at the same time every day. Something was happening in the dark. On Wednesday she set an alarm for four in the morning and crept out with a torch.

The pond was warm as bath water and perfectly flat. Not a ripple moved. She knelt on the edge and shone the torch along the boxes. Most crabs sat still on the bottom. But one crab was doing something odd. He had climbed up the side of his box until his eyes were just above the water. At his mouth, a froth of tiny bubbles grew and popped, grew and popped.
'He's breathing,' whispered Anjana. But crabs have no noses. Where was he getting air?

Then she remembered Miss Radha, her science teacher. Miss Radha had held up a picture of a crab with the side of her shell lifted off. Underneath lay rows of soft, feathery gills. 'A crab breathes the air that is mixed into the water,' Miss Radha had said. 'But water holds very little. And the crab can only use what is touching her gills. She has to keep new water coming.'

Anjana looked at her pond. Nothing was moving, and nothing had moved for days. Ammamma had shut the gate on Sunday because a neighbour told her wild fish came in on the tide and ate the crab food. For three nights the water had stood still. It was warm, and warm water holds even less air. Twenty-four crabs were breathing it. Even the green weed was breathing it at night, when the weed could not make any air in the dark.
'The air in the water is running out,' said Anjana aloud. 'And it is lowest of all just before sunrise.'
She ran to the gate. The beam was heavy, and the wood was wet and swollen. She pulled with all her strength and it did not move. 'Ammamma!' she shouted. 'Ammamma, please! The crabs can't breathe!'
Ammamma came out in her nightdress, rubbing her eyes. 'Can't breathe? They live in water, child.' 'Water with no air in it,' said Anjana. 'Please. Help me lift the gate.'

Ammamma looked at her granddaughter's face for a moment. Then she took hold of the beam. Together they heaved it up. The tide was nearly full. The backwater came pouring in, cool and moving, smelling of mud and salt. It slid across the pond and the boxes began to rock.

Anjana ran back to the crab with the bubbles. For a while nothing changed. Then, slowly, the froth thinned. The crab slid down the side of his box. His claws loosened and he sank into the water, calm and quiet.
The sun came up over the coconut palms. No more crabs floated that day. From then on, Ammamma opened the gate at every high tide, and stretched a net across the opening to keep the wild fish out.
A week later, Ammamma took the red thread off the post. 'So it was not luck,' she said. 'It was air.' 'It was both,' said Anjana. 'We were lucky to have a tide.'
story.epiphany: A crab takes air from the water, but still water near her gills runs out of air, and warm water holds little to start with. Only new, moving water brings more.
ask: Why did the crabs rise to the top of their boxes before dawn?
What could Ammamma do to keep the water fresh, if she still wanted to keep wild fish out?
Why would warm water make the problem worse?
