roots.context: We have followed oxygen into worms, ants, crabs, snails and spiders. Now we ask what this tells us about all bodies, including our own.

deep_truth.truth: In the jelly cubes, the colour crept in only a few millimetres, however big the cube. Oxygen drifts through a body in the same slow way. So every animal is built to keep the outside world close to every part of their body. Gills, air tubes and lungs are all that one job.
deep_truth.habit: We say an animal breathes with their lungs, as if breathing happened in one organ. But every cell needs oxygen, so breathing happens everywhere. A lung or a gill is a way of folding the outside deep into the body.
deep_truth.evidence: In Colour Cubes, the thin slice was coloured right through, but the big cube still had a white middle after 40 minutes. Drifting alone cannot reach the middle of a thick body. Worms stay thin, crabs fold gills, and ants branch tubes to every part.

three.who_am_i: Inside you, thin folded lungs bring the air close to your blood. You are built round the same short distance as an ant or a crab.
three.what_is_life: A living body is always taking in air or water and giving some back. A worm, an ant and a crab each do this all day, with skin, tubes and gills.
three.what_is_this_world: The oxygen in the air was made by plants and tiny sea microbes. Every animal, from the ant to the crab, lives on air that other living beings made.

roots.thread: Oxygen is the same everywhere. A worm's skin, a crab's gill and an ant's tube all let oxygen drift through a thin, wet wall. The oxygen does not change. What changes is the body, built in a different shape to bring it in. One kind of air, and many kinds of bodies, each shaped around the same short distance. The edge between a body and the air turns out to be folded, stretched and branched, so it reaches almost everywhere inside.

teachings.teaching: The faculties of a body, such as speech, mind, eye and ear, once argued about which of them was most important. Prana, the breath, began to leave the body, and all the others were pulled with it. They agreed that breath is the chief.
teachings.link: Every part of an animal's body depends on oxygen arriving, whether the animal is a crab or a person.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka told his son that if life leaves one branch of a great tree, that branch dries up. If life leaves the whole tree, the whole tree dries up. Life moves through the whole tree.
teachings.link: Life moves through a whole body, not just one part, and oxygen has to reach every part for that to be true.

teachings.source: Tattvartha Sutra of Umasvati, chapter 2, verse 23
teachings.teaching: The Jain teacher Umasvati listed living beings by the number of senses. He named worms, ants, bees and people as examples of beings with two, three, four and five senses.
teachings.link: Jain teaching has long said that small animals such as worms and ants are living beings who feel, and deserve care.

science.text: Oxygen moves into animals by diffusion across thin, wet surfaces, and diffusion time grows with the square of the distance.
Giant insects once lived when the air held more oxygen. Whether oxygen allowed their size is argued over.

other_view.view: A gill or a tube is a tool that natural selection shaped step by step, because animals with a better air supply left more young. 'The outside folded in' is a useful way to picture it, they say, but nothing planned it.

practice.title: Breath at the edge
practice.say: Sit still and hold one hand in front of your nose. Breathe out and feel the warm air on your hand. Breathe in and feel the cooler air. Now picture the air reaching your fingertips and your toes, all the way to your smallest parts. An ant does this with no lungs at all. Ask yourself, where does the air stop and I begin?
practice.kid: Sit still and hold one hand near your nose. Breathe out and feel the warm air. Breathe in and feel the cool air. Now think of an ant breathing too.

ask: If every cell breathes, where does your breath really go?
A worm breathes through her skin and an ant through tubes. Are they breathing the same air we do?
The oxygen you breathe was made by plants and tiny microbes. Whose breath are you breathing?
Is a crab's gill part of the crab, or part of the sea?
roots.art: An ant, a crab and a child, each cut open to show thin lines of air reaching every part of their bodies from the outside.

games.title: Wobbly Walk: an oxygen particle on its way to the middle
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent, or with friends
games.context: This is a coin game. A token wanders by chance, step by step, from the outside edge to a hungry cell inside. It shows why drifting is slow and why long distances take so much longer.

setup.art: A paper strip of nine squares numbered 0 to 8, with a token on square 0 and a coin beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Make a strip of nine squares, numbered 0 to 8. Square 0 is the outside air.

setup.art: A hand flipping a coin, with heads moving the token one square in and tails moving it one square back.
setup.caption: 2. Flip the coin. Heads, move in. Tails, move back.

setup.art: A score sheet with three rows for 'flat worm', 'ant' and 'crab', each with spaces for flips.
setup.caption: 3. Count your flips until the token reaches the target cell.

printables.title: 9 squares: a strip from the outside (0) to the deepest cell (8)
A score sheet with a row for each body and three tries
items: Flat worm, target square 2: try 1 ___ try 2 ___ try 3 ___ total ___
Ant, target square 4: try 1 ___ try 2 ___ try 3 ___ total ___
Crab, target square 8: try 1 ___ try 2 ___ try 3 ___ total ___
Crab with a pump, target square 8: try 1 ___ try 2 ___ try 3 ___ total ___

rules: Each player has a token and a coin. Put the token on square 0, the outside air.
Flip the coin. If it is heads, move the token one square towards the middle. If it is tails, move it one square back towards the outside. If you are on square 0 and flip tails, stay on 0.
Count every flip. Stop when the token reaches the target square for your body.
A flat worm's target is square 2, an ant's is square 4, and a crab's is square 8.
Play each body three times. Add up the flips. The body with the fewest flips is the easiest to reach.
In the pump round, a crab flips again, but heads now moves the token two squares in. This is a gill bailer or a heart pushing the oxygen along.
To win, be the player whose crab with a pump needs the fewest flips in total. If you play alone, try to beat your own total.

flow.do: Draw the strip of nine squares and number them 0 to 8. Give each player a small token and a coin. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: A particle of oxygen wanders by chance. Heads, one step in. Tails, one step back. It starts outside. About how many flips will it take to reach square two, square four and square eight?
flow.kid: Oxygen wanders by chance. How many flips to reach squares 2, 4 and 8?

ask.q: Square 2 takes a few flips. How many do you think to reach square 4, and square 8?
good: About twice as many for square 4.
Many more than that, because it wanders back.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write each guess on the score sheet. The long-run averages are about 6 flips for square 2, 20 for square 4, and 72 for square 8.
flow.context: This is the first step of Wobbly Walk. You guess before you play.

flow.do: Play the flat worm three times. Flip the coin, move the token, and count the flips until it reaches square 2. Write the three counts on the sheet.
flow.say: Start on square zero. Flip the coin. Heads, one step in. Tails, one step back. Count every flip until you reach square two. Do it three times.
flow.kid: Flat worm. Reach square 2. Count your flips. Do it three times.
flow.context: In this step, you play the flat worm, the shortest trip.

flow.do: Play the ant three times. Count the flips until the token reaches square 4. Write the counts down and add them.
flow.say: Now the ant. The target is square four. Count your flips each time. Do it three times and add them up.
flow.kid: Ant. Reach square 4. Count your flips. Do it three times.

ask.q: The ant's square is twice as far as the worm's. Did it take twice as many flips?
good: No. It took about three times as many or more.
It took much more than double.

check.q: Square 4 is twice as far as square 2. About how many times as many flips did it take?
check.why: Twice as far takes about four times as long, because each step forward can be undone by a step back. The averages are about 6 flips for square 2 and 20 for square 4, which is between 3 and 4 times more. A pick of 'twice' is the common first guess, because it treats the walk like a straight run.

flow.context: In this step, you play the ant, a longer trip.

flow.do: Play the crab three times. Count the flips until the token reaches square 8. This takes a long time, so stop at 100 flips and write 'more than 100'. Add up your counts.
flow.say: Now the crab. The target is square eight. This is a long walk. If you pass a hundred flips, stop and write more than a hundred.
flow.kid: Crab. Reach square 8. Stop at 100 flips if you must.
flow.parent: The average is about 72 flips, but one try can take over 200. That is why we stop at 100. A very long wander shows chance, and also why the ant and the crab cannot rely on drifting alone.
flow.context: In this step, you play the crab, a very long trip.

flow.do: Play the crab with a pump. Heads now moves two squares in. Tails still moves one back. Play three times and count the flips.
flow.say: Now give the crab a pump. Heads moves two squares in. Tails still moves one back. How many flips now? Do it three times.
flow.kid: Crab with a pump. Heads moves two in. Count your flips.

ask.q: What changed when the crab got a pump?
good: It reached square 8 in far fewer flips.
The wandering had a push in one direction.

flow.think: A crab's gill bailer and an insect's pumping belly both give a push in one direction. What would happen without it?
flow.parent: With the pump the average falls to about 14 flips. The coin is still random, but the push gives a direction.
flow.context: In this step, you add a pump and see how much it changes the trip.

flow.do: Add up the flips for each body. Write the totals, and compare. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at your totals. When the trip got twice as long, how did the number of flips change? What did the pump do?
flow.kid: Compare your totals. What did doubling the distance do? What did the pump do?

ask.q: When the distance doubled, how did the number of flips change?
good: It went up about four times.
It went up more than double.

flow.think: Why do ants and crabs not rely on wandering alone for their oxygen?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the totals and think about distance and pumps.

games.title: Air Route: how does this animal breathe?
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent, or with friends
games.context: This is a guessing game with 20 animals. For each card you pick how the animal gets air, then check the back and say why.

setup.art: Twenty cards in a pile in the middle of a table, and five route cards face up: skin, gills, air tubes, book lungs, lung.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the animal cards and the five route cards. Shuffle the animal cards.

setup.art: One child reading an animal card aloud while the other players each put a route card face down in front of them.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else picks a route card.

setup.art: Players turning their route cards over together, with the reader showing the back of the animal card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn your cards over together. The reader shows the back.

printables.title: 20 two-sided cards: an animal on the front and the way she breathes on the back

items.b: Skin. Her thin, wet skin lets oxygen drift in.
Skin. She is so thin that oxygen reaches every cell.

items.f: A jellyfish drifting in the sea.
items.b: Skin. Her body is almost all water, with only thin layers of living cells, so oxygen drifts in all over.
Air tubes. Air goes in through holes in her sides and along tubes to every part.
Air tubes. She pumps her belly to push air along her tubes while she flies.
Air tubes. A row of holes down each side leads to branching tubes.
Air tubes. Each body ring has holes that lead into tubes.
Air tubes. She carries a bubble of air under her wing covers, and her tubes open into it.

items.f: A mosquito larva hanging at the top of a pond.
items.b: Air tubes. She hangs at the top so her air tubes can touch the air.

items.f: A mud crab in a backwater.
items.b: Gills. Feathery gills under her shell take oxygen from the water.
Gills. She beats a small flap near her mouth to pull water over her gills.
Gills. She draws water through her body to breathe and to feed.

items.f: A young dragonfly in a pond.
items.b: Gills. They are inside her tail end, and she squirts water in and out.
Gills. She pumps water over them, and pushes it out through a tube.
Gills. She has gill-like plates under her tail that must stay damp.

items.f: A house spider on a web.
items.b: Book lungs. Thin plates inside her belly, like the pages of a book.
Book lungs. She has four pairs of them under her body.

items.f: A garden snail on a wall.
items.b: Lung. She has a pocket under her shell with a small opening, the breathing pore.

items.f: A pond snail that swims up to the surface.
items.b: Lung. She comes up to fill her lung with air.

items.f: A coconut crab on a palm in the Andaman Islands.
items.b: Lung. Her gill chamber works like a lung. She breathes air and would drown in deep water.

printables.title: 5 route cards: skin, gills, air tubes, book lungs and lung

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top animal card and reads the front aloud, without showing the back.
Every other player puts one route card face down. Then everyone turns their cards over together.
The reader reads the back aloud. Each player who picked the right route scores 1 point.
Score 1 extra point if you can say why that route suits the animal, for example why a jellyfish needs no gills.
Take turns being the reader. When all twenty cards are used, the highest score wins.
If you play alone, pick a route card, say why, then check the back. Count how many of the twenty you got right, and try to beat your score next time.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 animal cards and the 5 route cards. Shuffle the animal cards. Give each player one of each route card.
flow.say: These cards show animals without backbones. Each player gets five route cards: skin, gills, air tubes, book lungs and lung. We will guess how each animal gets air.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Take one of each route card.
flow.context: This is the first step of Air Route. You set up the cards.

flow.do: Play the first ten cards. After each card, read the back aloud. After card five, ask the question below.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone picks a route card. Turn them over together. Then the reader reads the back. Who got it? Who can say why?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a route card. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: What do the skin breathers have in common?
good: They are thin or small.
They live where it is wet.
None of them is thick.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first ten cards.

flow.do: Play the next ten cards. Keep the scores. After the last card, ask the question below.
flow.say: Play the next ten cards in the same way. Remember to say why when you can. Add up your scores at the end.
flow.kid: Play the last ten cards. Add up your points.

ask.q: Which animals surprised you?
good: The coconut crab breathes air.
The snail has a lung.
A dragonfly young has gills inside her tail.

check.q: A big animal needs more help to get oxygen to the middle of its body than a tiny one does. Which animal on the cards is a big crab that breathes air, even though most crabs breathe water?
check.why: The coconut crab is a crab, a group that mostly breathes water with gills, yet she lives on land and breathes air with a lung-like organ. The mud crab and the prawn both breathe water with gills.

flow.context: In this step, you play the last ten cards.

flow.do: Say who won. Ask your child which animal was hardest to guess, and why.
flow.say: Who got the most points? Which card was the hardest to guess? Why was it hard?
flow.kid: Who won? Which card was hardest? Why?
flow.think: Which animal would change her route if she lived in a different place?
flow.context: This is the last step of Air Route. You look back at the game.

experiments.title: Colour Cubes: how far does colour creep into jelly?
experiments.question: A thin slice, a small cube and a big cube of clear jelly sit in coloured water for 40 minutes. Which will be coloured right through to the middle?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which piece will be coloured all the way through, and which will keep a clear middle? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All the pieces are cut from the same jelly. They sit in the same bowl of colour for the same time. Only the size and shape of the piece changes, so any difference in how far the colour reaches comes from the size. Cutting one spare big cube open after 10 minutes also shows how the colour creeps as time passes.
results_table: Width of coloured edge on the cut face (millimetres)

materials.item: 2 level teaspoons of agar-agar (China grass) powder. If you have strands, use about 10 grams
500 millilitres of water and a pan
a clean steel box or tray about 15 by 12 centimetres, at least 3 centimetres deep
a sharp knife, a chopping board and a ruler marked in millimetres
liquid food colour, red or blue
a deep bowl, a spoon and a timer
kitchen paper, and paper and a pencil for notes

experiments.safety: A grown-up must boil the agar and use the knife. Hot jelly burns like hot water. Food colour stains hands and clothes, so wear an old shirt. Do not eat the coloured jelly.
experiments.record: Fill in the table for each piece. Write the width of the coloured edge and the width of the clear middle in millimetres. Then write what you think, what you saw and why.
experiments.context: In this test you make clear jelly, cut it into three shapes, and soak them in colour. You find out how far colour creeps in, in 10 and in 40 minutes.

setup.art: A pan of water on a stove with a spoon stirring in white agar powder, and a steel box ready beside it.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up boils water with agar. Pour it into a steel box and let it set.

setup.art: A block of clear jelly on a chopping board being cut into a thin slice, a 1 centimetre cube and two 2 centimetre cubes, with a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Cut a thin slice, a small cube and two big cubes.

setup.art: Four pieces of jelly sitting in a bowl of red water, with a timer showing 40 minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Put the pieces into strong colour. Start the timer.

setup.art: A jelly cube cut in half, showing a thin red edge around a clear middle, with a ruler measuring the red edge.
setup.caption: 4. Cut each piece open. Measure the coloured edge and the clear middle.

flow.do: Show your child the agar, the box and the food colour. Say that clear jelly will be cut into three shapes. Write down their guess and their reason.
flow.say: We will make clear jelly. Then we will cut a thin slice, a small cube and a big cube. We will soak them in colour. Which piece will be coloured all the way through? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Jelly in colour. Which piece will be coloured all through? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that piece will be coloured all the way through?
good: It is the smallest, so the colour has less far to go.
It is thin, so the colour comes in from both sides.
The colour will go into all of them the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of Colour Cubes. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up pours 500 millilitres of water into a pan and stirs in 2 level teaspoons of agar powder. Boil for 2 minutes, stirring. Pour into the steel box, about 2.5 to 3 centimetres deep.
flow.say: A grown-up boils the water and the agar for two minutes. Then we pour it into the box. It will turn into firm, clear jelly as it cools.
flow.kid: A grown-up boils the agar. Pour it into the box. Let it cool.
flow.parent: If you have strands of China grass, soak 10 grams in the water for 10 minutes, then boil until no strands are left. Use the fridge to set it faster, 15 to 20 minutes. If your jelly is still soft after cooling, boil a new batch with another half teaspoon of powder. Plain gelatin jelly will also work if it is kept cold, but it melts in a warm room.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up makes the clear jelly.

flow.do: Wait about 15 minutes in the fridge, or 30 minutes in a cool room, until the jelly is firm. Tilt the box a little. The jelly should not run. While you wait, ask the question below.
flow.say: While the jelly sets, think about this. Where have you seen something spread out slowly, and where have you seen it spread fast?
flow.kid: Wait for the jelly to set. Think of things that spread slowly or fast.

ask.q: Where have you seen something spread slowly, and where fast?
good: Smell of food spreading across a room.
Ink or tea spreading in water.
A drop of dye on a wet cloth.

flow.parent: This is waiting time. Use it for the guess and for the question. Do not explain yet.
flow.context: This is waiting time while the jelly sets.

flow.do: A grown-up runs a knife round the edge and tips the jelly onto the board. Cut one thin slice 0.5 centimetres thick and 3 centimetres across. Cut one 1 centimetre cube. Cut two 2 centimetre cubes.
flow.say: A grown-up cuts the jelly. One thin slice. One small cube. Two big cubes. We keep one big cube as a spare. Measure each side with the ruler.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts a thin slice, a small cube and two big cubes.

check.q: Why do we cut all the pieces from the same jelly?
options: So the only difference between them is size and shape
check.why: If the jellies were different, we would not know if the colour went in differently because of the size or because of the jelly. The same jelly makes it a fair test.

flow.parent: The big cube must be a true 2 centimetre cube. Cut straight down. If the pieces break, cut new ones from the leftover jelly.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up cuts the jelly into the pieces you will test.

flow.do: Use a bowl about 12 centimetres across. Pour in 300 millilitres of water, enough to cover the big cubes. Stir in 2 teaspoons of food colour until the water is strongly coloured. Slide all four pieces in with a spoon, so none touch. Start the timer.
flow.say: Make the water a strong colour. Slide all four pieces in together. Start the timer. We will cut the spare big cube open after 10 minutes.
flow.kid: Make strong colour water. Slide in all four pieces. Start the timer.
flow.parent: Use the spoon, not fingers, so the jelly does not break. The pieces need to be under the colour, so use a deep bowl and, if needed, a bit more coloured water.
flow.context: In this step, you put the pieces into the colour and start the clock.

flow.do: Wait for 10 minutes. Lift out the spare big cube with the spoon. Dip it quickly in plain water and blot it dry. A grown-up cuts it in half. Measure the coloured edge on the cut face in millimetres. Write it down. Put the other pieces back.
flow.say: After ten minutes, take out the spare big cube. A grown-up cuts it in half. How far in did the colour go? Measure it.
flow.kid: Wait 10 minutes. Take out the spare cube. Cut it in half. Measure the colour.

ask.q: How far in did the colour go after 10 minutes, and what is in the middle?
good: A thin coloured edge, about 1 to 2 millimetres.
The middle is still clear.

flow.parent: After 10 minutes you will probably see a thin coloured edge, about 1 or 2 millimetres, and a clear middle. If you see nothing, give it another 5 minutes and add more food colour to the bowl. Cut with one clean downward press and wipe the knife each time, or the knife drags colour across the clear middle.
flow.context: In this step, you cut the spare big cube open after 10 minutes.

flow.do: Wait until the timer reaches 40 minutes. Use the time to do the Ring or Core activity if you have not yet done it. Then lift the other three pieces out, blot them, and keep them in a row in order of size.
flow.say: While you wait, do Ring or Core. When forty minutes are up, lift out the three pieces and line them up.
flow.kid: Wait to 40 minutes. Do Ring or Core. Then lift out the pieces.
flow.parent: This is waiting time, about 30 minutes in all. Ring or Core uses squared paper and fits well here.
flow.context: This is waiting time while the colour creeps in.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts each piece in half. Look at each cut face. Measure the coloured edge and the clear middle, in millimetres. Write both numbers in the table, and write yes if it is coloured right through.
flow.say: Now cut each piece in half. Look at the cut face. Measure the coloured edge. Measure the clear middle. Which piece is coloured right through?
flow.kid: Cut each piece in half. Measure the edge and the clear middle.

check.q: The colour went about the same distance into the small and the big cube. What does this show?
options: Colour creeps in about the same distance, so a big piece keeps a clear middle
Big cubes soak up colour faster
Colour only goes into small things
check.why: The edge was about the same width on every piece. The small cube and the slice were short enough to be coloured right through, but the big cube was too wide, so it kept a clear middle. A pick of 'faster' means you may have looked at the surface only.

flow.parent: Expect the slice to be coloured right through, the small cube to have a small clear middle, and the big cube to have a large clear middle. The edge is often 2 to 4 millimetres after 40 minutes. If the big cube is coloured all through, your colour is very strong or the jelly is soft. Write exactly what you see.
flow.context: In this step, you cut the pieces open and measure them.

flow.do: Compare the edge at 10 minutes and at 40 minutes on the big cube. Then ask your child to write what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Look at the big cube at ten minutes and at forty minutes. The time was four times as long. Was the edge four times as thick? What did you think, what did you see, and why?
flow.kid: Compare 10 and 40 minutes. Write what you think, saw and why.

ask.q: Was the edge four times thicker after four times as long?
good: No. It was only about twice as thick.
It slowed down.

flow.think: If the colour only reaches a few millimetres in 40 minutes, how long might it take to reach 2 centimetres?
flow.parent: This is the key finding. The edge grows more slowly than the time. Four times as long gives about twice as deep. Do not explain it yet. Let the child say what they notice. The explanation card and the Wobbly Walk game follow.
flow.context: In this step, you compare your results and write what you think, saw and why.

experiments.title: Sugar Lumps: does more outside dissolve faster?
experiments.question: The same amount of sugar is used as a whole lump, in broken pieces, or as powder. Which dissolves fastest in still water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which sugar will vanish first, and which will take the longest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each glass has the same amount of cool water from the same jug, and the same amount of sugar. Nobody stirs. Only the shape of the sugar changes, so any difference in time comes from the shape.
results_table: Time to vanish, try 1 (minutes and seconds)

materials.item: 6 sugar cubes, or 6 equal lumps of rock sugar (kalkandu)
6 matching glasses
a jug of cool tap water
a clean cloth and the back of a spoon
a timer and a pencil

experiments.safety: Tapping sugar with a spoon is safe, but a grown-up should help if you use hard rock sugar.
experiments.record: For each kind of sugar, write the time taken for no grains to be seen. If the whole lump is not gone after 10 minutes, write 'more than 10'.
experiments.context: In this test you dissolve the same sugar as a whole lump, in pieces and as powder, to see whether more outside makes it faster.

setup.art: Three glasses of water in a row, one with a whole sugar cube, one with broken pieces, and one with powder, all at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Set three glasses with the same amount of water.

setup.art: A sugar cube wrapped in a cloth being tapped gently with the back of a spoon.
setup.caption: 2. Break one cube into pieces, and crush one cube to powder.

setup.art: Three hands dropping the three kinds of sugar into three glasses at the same moment while a timer starts.
setup.caption: 3. Drop all three in at once. Do not stir. Start the timer.

setup.art: A child looking at the side of a glass to check whether any sugar remains at the bottom.
setup.caption: 4. Look from the side. Write the time when no grains are left.

flow.do: Show your child the three kinds of sugar. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: We have the same amount of sugar three ways. One lump, a few bits and some powder. Which will vanish first in still water? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Same sugar in three shapes. Which vanishes first? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will vanish first?
good: It is in the smallest bits.
The water touches more of it.
It is the quickest to melt.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sugar Lumps. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Wrap one cube in a cloth. Tap it gently with the back of a spoon until it breaks into about 8 pieces. Wrap another cube and crush it to powder. Keep the third whole. Fill three glasses with 150 millilitres of cool water each.
flow.say: Break one cube into bits. Crush one cube to powder. Keep one whole. Fill three glasses with the same amount of water.
flow.kid: Break one cube. Crush one. Keep one whole. Fill three glasses.

check.q: Why must all three glasses have the same amount of water, and the same amount of sugar?
options: So that only the shape of the sugar is different
So the sugar tastes the same
check.why: If the water or sugar were different, we would not know whether the shape made the difference. Changing one thing at a time makes it a fair test.

flow.parent: Use one cube for each. The broken and crushed sugar must weigh the same as the whole one, so do not lose any pieces from the cloth.
flow.context: In this step, you get the three kinds of sugar ready.

flow.do: Drop all three kinds of sugar into the three glasses at the same moment. Do not stir. Start the timer. Look from the side. Write the time when no grains are left at the bottom.
flow.say: Drop all three in together. Do not stir. Start the timer. Watch from the side. Write down when each one has vanished.
flow.kid: Drop all three in. Do not stir. Start the timer. Watch.

ask.q: Which vanished first, and which last? What do you notice?
good: The powder vanished fastest.
The whole lump took the longest.

flow.parent: Powder often vanishes in a few minutes, even unstirred. Broken pieces take longer. A whole lump can take more than ten minutes in still, cool water. If a lump is not gone after 10 minutes, stop and write 'more than 10'.
flow.context: In this step, you run the test and time how long each kind of sugar takes.

flow.do: Repeat with fresh glasses, fresh water and fresh sugar. Write the second times in the table. Work out the average for each.
flow.say: Do it all again with new glasses. Why do you think we repeat it? Write the second times down.
flow.kid: Do it again with new glasses. Write the new times.

check.q: Why do we repeat the test?
options: One try can be a fluke, so a second try makes us surer
Because the first result is always wrong
check.why: A single try can be unusual because of a draught, a bit of stirring, or a different lump. If the second result agrees, we can trust the pattern more.

flow.context: In this step, you repeat the test to check it.

flow.do: Ask your child to write what they thought, what they saw and why. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: What did you think, what did you see, and why? A crab's gill is shaped like a feather, not like a lump. Why might that help?
flow.kid: Write what you thought, saw and why. Why is a gill like a feather?

ask.q: Why might a crab's gill be shaped like a feather and not like a lump?
good: A feather shape has more outside to touch the water.
More of the gill meets the water, so oxygen gets in faster.

flow.think: What would a lump-shaped gill be like?
flow.parent: The sugar and the gill are different, but the idea is the same. More surface touching the water means faster change. Do not explain more than this yet.
flow.context: In this step, you write your result and think about gills.

experiments.title: Drop and Stir: why do crabs move water over their gills?
experiments.question: A drop of food colour is put into still cold water, still warm water and stirred cold water. Which glass becomes evenly coloured first?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which glass will be an even colour first, and which last? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each glass has the same amount of water and the same amount of food colour, put in the same way. Only one thing differs: whether the water is still or stirred, and warm or cold. The cold still glass is the control.

materials.item: 3 matching clear glasses
cold tap water and warm water that is comfortable to touch, about 40 degrees
liquid food colour
a teaspoon, a timer and a pencil
a white sheet of paper to put behind the glasses

experiments.safety: The warm water must be comfortable to touch, not hot. A grown-up should pour any water from a kettle. Wipe spills so nobody slips.
experiments.record: In each box of the table, write in words what you see: colour in a streak, colour at the bottom, colour spread evenly, and so on. Draw each glass after 10 minutes.
experiments.context: In this test you put colour in still and stirred water and watch how it spreads, to see why crabs and prawns pump water over their gills.

setup.art: Three clear glasses in a row in front of a white sheet of paper, labelled still cold, still warm and stirred cold.
setup.caption: 1. Fill three glasses with the same amount of water.

setup.art: A spoon touching the surface of the water and letting one drop of food colour fall in.
setup.caption: 2. Put one drop of food colour in each glass in the same way.

setup.art: A spoon stirring the third glass gently for three turns while the other two stand still.
setup.caption: 3. Stir only the third glass for three turns. Leave the others still.

setup.art: Three glasses after 10 minutes, one with a thin streak, one with a patchy cloud, and one evenly coloured.
setup.caption: 4. Watch each glass and write what you see.

flow.do: Show your child the three glasses. Glass A is cold and still. Glass B is warm and still. Glass C is cold and will be stirred. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: One drop of colour goes in each glass. One cold and still, one warm and still, one cold and stirred. Which will have an even colour first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Colour in three glasses. Which spreads evenly first? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that glass will be even first?
good: Stirring moves the colour all round.
Warm water spreads things faster.
Still water will take a long time.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Drop and Stir. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Put the white paper behind the glasses. Pour 200 millilitres of cold water into glasses A and C. Pour 200 millilitres of warm water into glass B. Let all three stand until the water stops moving.
flow.say: Pour the same amount of water into each. Two cold, one warm. Wait until nothing in the water is moving.
flow.kid: Pour the water into three glasses. Wait until the water is still.
flow.parent: A grown-up should check the warm water is comfortable, not hot. The glasses must be still before the drops go in, or the test is not fair.
flow.context: In this step, you get the three glasses ready.

flow.do: Touch the tip of a spoon to the surface of glass A. Let one drop of food colour fall in. Do the same for glass B and glass C. Start the timer. Now stir glass C three times, gently. Do not touch A or B again.
flow.say: One drop in each glass, in the same way. Start the timer. Now stir only the third glass three times.
flow.kid: Drop colour in each glass. Start the timer. Stir only glass C.

check.q: Why do we put the drop in each glass in the same way?
options: So the way we add the colour does not change the result
So the glasses look the same
So we use up the colour
check.why: If one drop were dropped from high up, it would push into the water and mix by itself. The same gentle drop in each glass keeps the test fair.

flow.context: In this step, you add the colour and stir only the third glass.

flow.do: Look at the glasses after 1 minute, after 5 minutes and after 10 minutes. Write what you see in words. Draw each glass at 10 minutes.
flow.say: Look after one minute, five minutes and ten minutes. Is the colour a streak, a cloud or even? Write it down.
flow.kid: Look at each glass after 1, 5 and 10 minutes. Write what you see.

ask.q: What is different about the stirred glass?
good: The colour spread much faster.
It was almost even after a short time.

flow.parent: Expect glass C to be much more even than the others within a minute. Glass A will be patchy for a long time, and its colour may sink to the bottom first. Glass B is usually quicker than A, because warm water rises and moves, but still patchier than C. If glass A is not even after 10 minutes, write 'not yet'.
flow.context: In this step, you watch and record how the colour spreads.

flow.do: Ask your child to write what they thought, what they saw and why. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: What did you think, what did you see, and why? A crab beats a flap near her mouth to pull water over her gills. Why would that help her?
flow.kid: Write what you thought, saw and why. How does stirring help a crab?

ask.q: How could moving water help a crab with her gills?
good: It brings new water with more air to the gills.
It stops the water near the gills running out of air.

flow.think: Warm water spreads colour faster. Is warm water better for a crab to breathe in?
flow.parent: Warm water mixes faster, but it holds less oxygen to begin with. That is why a hot, still pond is a double problem. Let the child think about it before you say this.
flow.context: In this step, you write your result and think about how crabs and prawns breathe.

activities.title: Ring or Core: how much of a body is near the edge?

materials.item: squared paper, or a plain page and a ruler
2 coloured pencils
a pencil

activities.context: In this activity you draw squares as flat 'bodies'. The edge cells touch the air, and the middle cells are far from it. You count each kind.

setup.art: Four squares drawn on squared paper, 2, 4, 6 and 8 squares wide, side by side.
setup.caption: 1. Draw squares that are 2, 4, 6 and 8 cells wide.

setup.art: The same four squares with the outside ring of cells coloured red and the middle cells coloured blue.
setup.caption: 2. Colour the outside ring red. Colour the middle blue.

setup.art: A table with columns for width, ring cells and middle cells, filled in for the four squares.
setup.caption: 3. Count each colour and fill in the table.

flow.do: Show your child the squared paper. Explain that each square is a flat body made of cells. The red cells at the edge touch the air. The blue cells in the middle do not. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: Each square is a flat animal made of cells. Cells at the edge touch the air. Cells in the middle do not. As the animal gets wider, which will grow faster, the edge or the middle?
flow.kid: A flat animal made of cells. Does the edge or the middle grow faster?

ask.q: When the animal gets wider, which grows faster, the edge cells or the middle cells? Why?
good: The middle, because it grows in two ways.
The edge, because it is on the outside.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it at the top of the page.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ring or Core. You guess before you count.

flow.do: Draw four squares: 2 cells wide, 4 cells wide, 6 cells wide and 8 cells wide. Colour the outside ring of cells red. Colour all the cells inside the ring blue. The smallest square is all red.
flow.say: Draw four squares. They are two, four, six and eight cells wide. Colour the outside ring red. Colour the middle blue.
flow.kid: Draw squares 2, 4, 6 and 8 wide. Red edge, blue middle.
flow.parent: A 2 by 2 square has no middle at all. That is correct. If counting is slow, let your child count along a row and use the rule: ring = 4 times the width minus 4.
flow.context: In this step, you draw and colour the squares.

flow.do: Count the red cells and the blue cells in each square. Write them in a table with three columns: width, red cells and blue cells. You should find 4 and 0, then 12 and 4, then 20 and 16, then 28 and 36.
flow.say: Count the red cells and the blue cells in each square. Write both numbers in the table.
flow.kid: Count red and blue in each square. Fill in the table.

ask.q: At which size do the blue cells first outnumber the red cells?
good: The 8 wide square.
Between 6 and 8.

check.q: A flat body is 10 cells wide. Which is bigger, its edge ring or its middle?
options: Its edge ring, with 40 cells against 60
check.why: A 10 wide square has 100 cells. The ring has 4 times 10 minus 4, which is 36 cells. The middle has 100 minus 36, which is 64 cells. In a wider body, most cells are far from the edge, and drifting oxygen has a long way to reach them.

flow.context: In this step, you count the cells and find the pattern.

flow.do: Ask your child what the middle cells would need if they were real cells. Read the answer from the table.
flow.say: Pretend each cell needs air all the time, and air only comes in from the edge. In the biggest square, what do the blue cells need?
flow.kid: Blue cells are far from the air. What do they need?

ask.q: What could help the blue cells get air?
good: A tube from the edge to the middle.
Thin folds so the edge is closer.
A pump to push air in.

flow.think: How would you make the blue cells in the 8 wide square closer to the air?
flow.parent: Accept any idea. Tubes, folds and pumps are all real. Do not explain yet. The explanation card comes later.
flow.context: In this step, you think about how the middle cells could be reached.

activities.title: Eight Blocks: which shape has the most outside?

materials.item: 8 identical cubes, such as sugar cubes, dice or small building blocks
paper and a pencil

activities.context: In this activity you build the same eight cubes into different shapes and count how many faces touch the air. It shows why gills and book lungs are folded and spread out.

setup.art: Eight cubes built into a solid 2 by 2 by 2 block on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Build a solid block, 2 cubes wide, 2 deep and 2 high.

setup.art: The same eight cubes in a flat layer, 2 cubes by 4 cubes, and then in a single long line.
setup.caption: 2. Rebuild them as a flat layer, and then as a long line.

setup.art: The eight cubes spread apart, one cube on its own in each spot.
setup.caption: 3. Spread all eight apart, so no two touch.

flow.do: Give your child eight cubes. Ask them to guess which shape will have the most faces touching the air.
flow.say: Here are eight cubes. We will build them four ways. Which way will have the most faces touching the air? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Eight cubes, four shapes. Which has most faces touching the air? Why?

ask.q: Which shape do you think has the most faces touching the air, and why?
good: The one spread apart, because every cube is alone.
The long line.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A face that touches another cube does not count. You may count the table side as a face in all four shapes, or leave it out. Be consistent. The numbers below count every face, even the one on the table, as if the shapes floated in the air.
flow.context: This is the first step of Eight Blocks.

flow.do: Build the solid block. Count every face that does not touch another cube. Write it down. Then do the same for the flat layer, the long line, and the eight cubes spread apart.
flow.say: Build each shape and count the faces that touch the air. Only count faces that are not touching another cube. Write each number down.
flow.kid: Build each shape. Count the faces that touch the air. Write them down.

ask.q: Which shape had the fewest faces touching the air, and which the most?
good: The solid block had the fewest.
The spread-out cubes had the most.

check.q: You should have found 24, 28, 34 and 48 faces. Which shape is the 24?
check.why: In a solid block, many faces press against other cubes, so only the outside faces count. The block has six sides of four faces each, which is 24. The same cubes spread apart each show all six faces, which is 48.

flow.parent: Solid 2 by 2 by 2 block: 24. Flat 2 by 4 layer: 28. Single line of 8: 34. All eight apart: 48. Same cubes, same amount of stuff, but twice as much outside when spread apart.
flow.context: In this step, you build the shapes and count the faces.

flow.do: Ask your child which shape is most like a crab's gill and which most like a solid lump. Ask why a gill is feathery.
flow.say: The same cubes gave a lot more outside when spread out. A crab's gill is a bit like the spread out cubes. Why might that help a crab?
flow.kid: Same cubes, more outside when spread. Why do gills spread like that?

ask.q: Why is a gill feathery and not a solid lump?
good: More of it touches the water.
More oxygen can get in at once.

flow.think: A book lung is a stack of thin plates. Which of your shapes is it more like?
flow.context: In this step, you link the blocks to gills and book lungs.

activities.title: Dry Finger: carrying a bubble of air under water

materials.item: a wide bowl of water
a small pinch of baby powder, or of finely ground black pepper
a dry towel

activities.safety: A grown-up should sprinkle the powder. Keep the powder away from your face. Do not blow on it or breathe it in, because it can irritate eyes, noses and lungs.
activities.context: In this activity a finger carries a layer of air under water. Some water beetles and water bugs carry air in just this way.

setup.art: A bowl of water with a thin dusting of white powder floating on the surface.
setup.caption: 1. Sprinkle a thin dusting of powder on the water.

setup.art: A finger being pushed slowly down through the powder into the water, with a silvery layer around it.
setup.caption: 2. Push a finger slowly down through the powder.

setup.art: A hand lifted out of the bowl with a dry, powdered finger next to a wet normal finger.
setup.caption: 3. Lift it out. Compare it with a finger put in without powder.

flow.do: Show your child the bowl and the powder. Ask what will happen to a finger pushed under the powder.
flow.say: I will sprinkle a little powder on the water. You will push one finger through it. What do you think your finger will look like under the water? Will it come out wet or dry? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A finger through powder, under water. Wet or dry? Why?

ask.q: Do you think your finger will come out wet or dry? Why?
good: Wet, because it was in water.
Dry, because the powder will cover it.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Dry Finger.

flow.do: A grown-up sprinkles a thin, even dusting of powder on the water. Push a finger slowly down through the powder and into the water. Look at it from the side.
flow.say: Push your finger slowly down through the powder. Look at it from the side. What do you see around it?
flow.kid: Push a finger down slowly. Look from the side. What do you see?

ask.q: What do you see around your finger under the water?
good: A silvery layer.
A shiny skin, like a mirror.

flow.parent: The silvery shine is a thin layer of air held against the finger by the powder. Without the powder, the water would soak the finger and no layer would form.
flow.context: In this step, you push a finger through the powder and look at the silvery layer.

flow.do: Lift the finger out slowly. Is it wet or dry? Feel it. Then put another finger in without powder and compare.
flow.say: Lift your finger out. Is it wet or dry? Now try a finger without powder. How are they different?
flow.kid: Lift it out. Wet or dry? Try a finger without powder.

ask.q: How was the powdered finger different from the plain one?
good: The powdered one stayed dry.
It had a layer of air around it.

check.q: A diving beetle carries a bubble of air under her wing covers when she dives. What does the air bubble do?
options: It gives her air to breathe under water
It makes her float like a cork
check.why: Her air tubes open into the bubble. She breathes the air from it, and the bubble also gets a little more oxygen from the water. A pick of 'float' is partly true, because air makes her lighter, but she uses it mainly to breathe.

flow.parent: Diving beetles and some water bugs trap air on hairs and under their wings. Some bugs keep a very thin layer of air on tiny hairs that works a little like a gill, because oxygen can drift from the water into the air layer as they use it.
flow.context: In this step, you compare a dry finger with a wet one and think about diving beetles.

activities.title: Gills in the Market, or a Picture Hunt

materials.item: a visit to a fish stall with a grown-up, or pictures of crabs, prawns and mussels from a book or a screen
a hand magnifying glass
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up goes with you to the stall. Do not touch live crab claws. Ask the seller before touching anything, and wash your hands afterwards. If anyone in the family has a shellfish allergy, or you do not eat fish, use pictures instead.
activities.context: In this activity you look for gills on a crab, a prawn or a fish, at a fish stall or in pictures, and compare them with an ant's breathing holes.

setup.art: A child with a grown-up at a fish stall looking at a crab on a tray.
setup.caption: 1. At the fish stall, look at a crab with a grown-up.

setup.art: A hand lifting the side flap of a crab's shell to show the gills underneath.
setup.caption: 2. Ask the seller to lift the side of the shell.

setup.art: A drawing of a crab's gills with labels for gill, shell and leg.
setup.caption: 3. Draw and label what you see.

flow.do: Tell your child that today you will look for gills. Ask where they think a crab's gills are.
flow.say: A crab has gills, but you cannot see them from outside. Where do you think they are hidden? Why?
flow.kid: Where are a crab's gills hidden? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Where do you think a crab keeps her gills?
good: Under her shell.
Near her mouth.
In her legs.

flow.parent: If you cannot visit a stall, search for pictures of a crab with the shell lifted. Both work. Do not correct the guess yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the gills hunt.

flow.do: At the stall, ask the seller if they can lift the side of the shell on a crab that has died. Look at the gills with the magnifier. Look at a prawn, a mussel or a fish too.
flow.say: Look at the gills. Are they smooth or feathery? What colour are they? Do they look like a lump or a comb?
flow.kid: Look at the gills. Are they feathery? Draw one.

ask.q: What do the gills look like?
good: Feathery.
Like a comb or a row of thin leaves.

flow.parent: Crab gills are grey to tan, and look like rows of thin leaves or a feather. Fish gills are red because of the blood close to the surface. Never handle a live crab's claws.
flow.context: In this step, you look closely at gills and compare them.

flow.do: Back home, draw what you saw and label it: gill, shell, leg. Then ask your child to compare the crab with an ant. Where does each one get air?
flow.say: Draw the gills and label them. An ant has no gills. Where does an ant get air, and how is she different from a crab?
flow.kid: Draw the gills. How is an ant different from a crab?

ask.q: How does an ant get air differently from a crab?
good: An ant has holes in her sides and air tubes.
A crab has gills and takes air from water.

flow.think: A crab on land keeps her gills wet. How can she do that?
flow.context: In this step, you draw the gills and compare a crab with an ant.

activities.title: Pipes or a Wet Sponge: two kinds of blood

materials.item: a bendy straw
a medicine syringe without a needle, or a small plastic squeezy bottle
a shallow tray and 5 small pieces of damp kitchen sponge
a cup of water with a few drops of food colour
a timer and a ruler

activities.context: In this activity you move coloured water two ways: pushed through a pipe, like closed blood, and soaked through a sponge, like open blood.

setup.art: A syringe full of red water joined to a straw with a clay seal, and the straw's far end over a cup.
setup.caption: 1. Join a syringe to a straw. This is the closed pipe.

setup.art: A tray with five damp sponge pieces in a line, touching end to end, and a small pool of red water at one end.
setup.caption: 2. Set sponge pieces in a row in a tray. This is the open soak.

setup.art: A timer next to the straw and the tray, with a child writing two times.
setup.caption: 3. Time how long the colour takes to reach the far end each way.

flow.do: Show your child the straw and the sponge pieces. Ask which will carry colour to the far end faster, and why.
flow.say: One way pushes colour through a pipe. One way lets it soak through sponge. Which gets to the far end first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pipe or sponge? Which carries colour to the far end faster? Why?

ask.q: Which do you think is faster, and why?
good: The pipe, because it goes straight.
The sponge, because it goes everywhere.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the two kinds of blood test.

flow.do: Fill the syringe with coloured water. Push it into one end of the straw, with a bit of clay round the join. Hold the far end over a cup. Push the plunger and time how long the colour takes to come out.
flow.say: Fill the syringe. Push the water through the straw. How many seconds before it comes out at the far end?
flow.kid: Push water through the straw. Time how long it takes.
flow.parent: Expect about a second. The pipe holds the liquid together, so a push at one end moves liquid at the far end almost at once. This is like closed blood.
flow.context: In this step, you time the closed pipe.

flow.do: Set the five damp sponge pieces, each about 3 centimetres long, in a row in the tray, touching end to end. Pour a spoon of coloured water at the first piece. Write down how long it takes the colour to reach each piece. Stop after 5 minutes.
flow.say: Pour a little colour on the first sponge. Watch it spread. Time how long until each sponge has colour. Stop after five minutes.
flow.kid: Pour colour on the first sponge. Time how far it spreads.

ask.q: How is the sponge different from the pipe?
good: It was much slower.
It reaches every sponge, but slowly.

flow.parent: The colour soaks from piece to piece slowly, and may not reach the last one in 5 minutes. This is like open blood: it can bathe every organ, but it is slow without a strong pump.
flow.context: In this step, you time the open soak.

flow.do: Ask your child why an ant can manage with open blood, but a large animal that runs fast cannot.
flow.say: Open blood reaches every part, but slowly. An ant is tiny. Why might open blood be good enough for an ant?
flow.kid: Open blood is slow. Why is it good enough for an ant?

ask.q: Why might open blood be good enough for an ant?
good: An ant is tiny, so nothing is very far away.
Her air tubes bring the oxygen, not her blood.

flow.think: What would a big, fast animal need instead?
flow.context: In this step, you think about when open blood works well.

projects.title: Air Tubes in a Roll: a model of an insect's breathing

materials.item: 1 cardboard roll from kitchen foil or cling film, about 30 centimetres long. A toilet roll is too short
4 drinking straws
4 small strips of tissue paper or thin kitchen paper, about 1 centimetre by 5 centimetres
modelling clay or play dough, a lump the size of a lime
sticky tape and scissors
a pencil to poke holes

projects.safety: A grown-up should help poke the holes in the roll and cut the straws.

schedule.what: Make the model. Test it. Block the tubes. Compare.

projects.record: Draw the model. Mark which paper strips moved when you blew, and which did not. Write one sentence on what each part of the model stands for.
projects.context: In this project you make a model of an insect's air tubes. You blow into one end, and see if a flutter reaches every paper strip at the end of a branch.

setup.art: A cardboard roll with four holes poked along its side, 4 centimetres apart.
setup.caption: 1. Poke four holes along the side of the roll.

setup.art: Four straws pushed into the holes and sealed with clay, each with a paper strip hanging at its end.
setup.caption: 2. Push a straw into each hole. Seal with clay. Hang a paper strip at each straw's end.

setup.art: A child blowing gently into one end of the roll while the other end is plugged with clay, and four paper strips fluttering.
setup.caption: 3. Plug the far end. Blow in at the near end. Watch the strips.

setup.art: The same model with one straw pinched shut and its paper strip hanging still.
setup.caption: 4. Pinch one straw shut. Blow again. What happens to that strip?

flow.do: Show your child the roll, the straws and the paper strips. Ask what will happen to the strips when they blow in at one end.
flow.say: This roll is the main air tube. The straws are branches. The paper strips are the cells that need air. If I blow into the roll, what will happen to the strips? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A roll with branches. Blow in. What happens to the paper strips? Why?

ask.q: Do you think all four strips will move? Why?
good: Yes, because air goes down all the straws.
Only the nearest one will move.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Air Tubes in a Roll.

flow.do: A grown-up pokes four holes along one side of the roll, 4 centimetres apart. Push a straw into each hole, about 2 centimetres in. Seal each joint with clay. Hang a paper strip at the end of each straw with tape. Plug one end of the roll with clay.
flow.say: Poke four holes along the roll. Push a straw into each one. Seal each with clay. Tape a paper strip beside each straw end. Plug one end of the roll.
flow.kid: Make four holes. Add four straws. Seal with clay. Tape on paper strips.
flow.parent: The clay must seal the joints, or air will escape. The paper strips must hang just in front of each straw end, where the air comes out.
flow.context: In this step, you build the model.

flow.do: Blow gently into the open end of the roll. Watch the four paper strips. Try it three times. Write down which strips moved each time.
flow.say: Blow in gently. Watch all four strips. Do they all move? Try it three times.
flow.kid: Blow into the roll. Do all four strips move?

ask.q: Did air reach all four strips? What does this tell you about branching tubes?
good: Yes. Branching tubes reach many places at once.
Even the far strip moved.

check.q: In the model, what does the blowing stand for?
options: An insect pumping her belly to push air along her tubes
A worm breathing through her skin
check.why: Blowing is the pump. A big insect pumps her belly to push air along her tubes, so air reaches the far parts faster than drifting alone would.

flow.context: In this step, you blow and watch which strips move.

flow.do: Pinch one straw shut and blow again. Then pinch two straws shut. Write what happens to the paper strips on those straws. Ask what could block an insect's holes.
flow.say: Pinch one straw shut. Blow again. What happens to its strip? Now pinch two. What happens?
flow.kid: Pinch a straw shut. Blow. What happens to that strip?

ask.q: What happens to a part of the body whose tube is blocked?
good: It gets no air.
That strip stops moving.

flow.think: Oil on an insect's holes can kill her. Why? What does the model tell you about why a big animal needs tubes?
flow.parent: A film of oil can block an insect's spiracles, which is one way some gardeners control pests. The same thing happens to the model when a straw is pinched. What does a blocked tube mean for the cells beyond it?
flow.context: In this step, you block a tube and see what happens.

challenges.title: The Fresh Tank: mix a drop of colour across the bowl, fast
challenges.problem: A bowl of still water has one drop of food colour at one end. Mix the colour right across the bowl in the shortest time you can. You may use things from the kitchen but not your hands, and you may not shake or tilt the bowl.
constraints: Use a bowl of water about 25 centimetres wide and 8 centimetres deep.
Put one drop of food colour at one end of the bowl.
Do not touch the water with your hands, and do not shake or tilt the bowl.
Time how long until the colour looks even from above.
materials: a spoon, a cup, a straw, a card, and a jug
general: Stir with a spoon in slow circles.
Pour water in from a jug held high, so it splashes in.
Blow through a straw into the water.
creative: Tape a card to a spoon to make a paddle, and push water from one end to the other, like a crab's gill bailer.
Use a cup to scoop water from the coloured end and pour it at the clear end, again and again.
Make a little waterfall from a paper cup with a hole in it, held above the bowl. A grown-up pokes the hole.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch two or three designs first. Test each and time it. Change one thing, such as the speed or the place, and test again. Which design mixed the colour fastest? Why do you think so?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about moving water. You find a way to spread colour across a bowl, as a crab moves water over her gills.

setup.art: A child sketching three designs on paper: a paddle, a pouring jug and a straw.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some ideas on paper.

setup.art: A bowl of water with a single drop of red colour at one end and a timer beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Put one drop of colour at one end of the bowl.

setup.art: A paddle made from a card sweeping water across the bowl, with red colour spreading out.
setup.caption: 3. Try your design and time it.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to sketch two or three different ways to mix the colour without touching the water.
flow.say: A crab moves water with a flap near her mouth. We want to move water across this bowl. How could you do it? Draw some ideas first.
flow.kid: Draw some ways to move the water across the bowl.

Pouring from high.
Blowing.

challenges.title: The Giant Insect: how will she breathe?
challenges.problem: Design an insect as long as your forearm, about 25 centimetres. Show how air will reach every part of her body. Where are her spiracles, her tubes and her pump?
constraints: Her body is 25 centimetres long and about 6 centimetres thick.
Every part of her body must be within 2 centimetres of a tube. This is a rule for the game, because real tubes reach much closer.
Draw her spiracles, her main tubes, her branches and anything else she needs.
Say how the air moves along the tubes.
general: Many spiracles along each side, with a thick main tube from each one.
A belly that squeezes and relaxes, like a bellows, to push air along the tubes.
Tubes that branch into finer and finer threads that reach every muscle.
creative: Add a sac of air near the middle that works as a store.
Give her flat, thin wings that carry air tubes of their own.
Make her live in water, with a long breathing tube like a snorkel.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your giant insect and mark where every cell can get air. Then ask what would go wrong if you made her twice as long. Do you need more tubes, a bigger pump, or something else?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about size and breathing. You draw a giant insect and show how air can reach all of her.
