flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to say what a giant insect would need that a tiny ant does not.
flow.say: An ant is tiny. This insect is as long as your arm. Tubes that work for an ant might not work for her. What might she need?
flow.kid: A giant insect needs more than an ant does. What?

ask.q: What might a giant insect need that an ant does not?
good: More tubes.
A pump to push the air.
Wider tubes.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Giant Insect challenge. You think about what she needs.

flow.do: Draw the insect. Mark spiracles, main tubes, branches and a pump. Write one sentence under each part saying what it does.
flow.say: Draw your insect. Draw her spiracles, her tubes and her pump. Write one sentence for each part.
flow.kid: Draw the insect. Add spiracles, tubes and a pump. Write what each does.
flow.context: In this step, you design your insect.

flow.do: Check the design with your child. Find the cell furthest from a tube. Is it within 2 centimetres? If not, add more tubes. Then ask what would go wrong if she were twice as long.
flow.say: Find the part of her body furthest from a tube. Is it close enough? If not, add more branches. What if she were twice as long?
flow.kid: Find the furthest part. Is it near a tube? Add more branches.

ask.q: What would go wrong if she were twice as long?
good: The middle would be too far from the tubes.
She would need many more tubes.

flow.think: Some scientists think tubes limit how big an insect can grow. Is that a good reason?
flow.context: In this step, you check the design and test it with a bigger size.

items.p: In Colour Cubes, the colour crept in about the same distance whatever the size of the piece. Why did the big cube keep a clear middle?
opts: The colour could not travel far enough into the middle in that time
The big cube was made of different jelly
Colour only goes into small things
items.why: The edge was about the same width on every piece. The middle of the big cube was too far from the edge for the colour to reach in 40 minutes. The jelly was the same, and colour does go into big things, just slowly.

items.p: A particle that drifts to a place twice as far takes about twice as long.
items.why: False. Drifting is a random wander, so each step forward can be undone by a step back. Twice as far takes about four times as long.

items.p: An earthworm has no lungs and no gills. How does she breathe?
items.why: Oxygen dissolves in the wet film on her skin and drifts in. She is thin, so every cell is close to the outside. She has no nose and no shell.

items.p: An insect breathes through tiny holes along her sides called ____.
items.why: Spiracles are the doorways. The air goes along tubes called tracheae, which branch to reach every cell.

items.p: Match each animal to how she gets air.
items.why: Each body suits its place. A thin worm uses her skin. A crab lives in water, so she uses gills. An ant and a spider live in air, so they use tubes and book lungs. A land snail keeps a wet pocket inside her shell.

items.p: Sort each animal by the main way she gets air.
items.why: Worms and flatworms are thin, so skin is enough. Crabs and prawns live in water and have gills. Caterpillars and bees have air tubes.

items.p: An insect's blood carries most of her oxygen to her cells.
items.why: False. Air tubes carry the oxygen straight to the cells. An insect's blood carries food and waste, and cells that fight germs.

items.p: A cube is 3 centimetres wide. It has 6 faces, and each face is 3 centimetres by 3 centimetres. How many square centimetres of outside does it have?
items.why: Each face is 3 times 3, which is 9 square centimetres. Six faces make 6 times 9, which is 54 square centimetres.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Earthworm, flatworm, jellyfish, ant.
items.a: Ant, because she breathes with air tubes. The other three breathe through their skin.
items.why: The earthworm, the flatworm and the jellyfish are thin, and oxygen drifts in all over their skin. The ant is thicker and uses tubes.

items.p: Why can a still, warm pond run short of air for its crabs and fish?
opts: Warm water holds less oxygen, and still water is not refreshed
Crabs only breathe in cold water
Warm water has no oxygen in it at all
items.why: Water holds only a little oxygen, and warm water holds even less. If it does not move, the animals use up what is next to them. A pick of 'no oxygen at all' goes too far, because warm water still holds some.

items.p: Put these in the right order to show how air reaches an ant's muscle cell.
a: Air goes in through a spiracle on her side
Air moves along a wide tube
The tube branches into finer tubes
Oxygen drifts the last tiny distance into a cell
items.why: Air enters at the spiracle and travels the long way along the tubes. Drifting is only used for the last tiny distance, where it is quick.

items.p: Write what you think, what you saw and why, for Colour Cubes. Use three sentences.
items.a: A strong answer says what they thought would happen, what they measured (a coloured edge of a few millimetres and a clear middle in the big cube), and why (colour drifts only a short way, so the middle of a big piece stays clear).
items.why: A good answer has a claim, evidence from the test with real numbers, and a reason that links them.

items.p: Why can a flat, thin worm breathe through her skin, but a big crab cannot?
items.a: Oxygen only drifts a short way. A thin worm has every cell close to the skin. A big crab has a middle far from the outside, so she needs gills to bring the water close.
items.why: A strong answer says that distance is the problem, and names the fix, such as gills.

items.p: Draw an ant. Show where the air goes in and how it reaches her legs.
items.a: An ant with holes along her sides, thick tubes running inward, and fine branches reaching the head, tummy and legs.
items.why: A strong drawing shows spiracles on the sides, tubes that branch into finer ones, and branches that reach the legs and head.

items.p: What does the gill bailer of a crab do?
opts: She pushes water over her gills
items.why: The gill bailer is a flap near her mouth that beats back and forth. It draws water past her gills so fresh water with new oxygen keeps arriving.

items.p: A coconut crab breathes air and would drown in deep water.
items.why: True. Her gill chamber has become lung-like. She is a crab, but a crab that breathes like a land animal.

items.p: A cube 1 centimetre wide has 6 square centimetres of outside and 1 cubic centimetre of inside. A cube 2 centimetres wide has 24 square centimetres outside and 8 cubic centimetres inside. How does the outside for each bit of inside change?
items.why: The small cube has 6 outside for 1 inside. The big cube has 24 outside for 8 inside, which is 3 for each. So each bit of inside has half as much outside.

items.p: A cube is 4 centimetres wide. How many square centimetres of outside does it have?
items.why: Each face is 4 times 4, which is 16 square centimetres. Six faces make 6 times 16, which is 96 square centimetres.

items.p: Going twice as far takes about ____ times as long.
items.why: Distance doubles, and the time goes up by 2 times 2, which is 4. This is true for drifting but not for walking in a straight line.

items.p: Air holds about 30 times more oxygen than the same amount of water. A crab needs the oxygen from 3 litres of air. About how much water must pass over her gills?
items.why: Water has about one-thirtieth the oxygen, so she needs about 30 times as much. 3 times 30 is 90 litres. This is why gills need a lot of moving water.

items.p: Cold water usually holds more dissolved oxygen than warm water.
items.why: True. Warm water holds less. A hot, still pond can run short of oxygen for the animals living in it.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: A tiny hole in an insect's side
A stack of thin plates inside a spider
A flap that pushes water over a crab's gills
The blood-like liquid of insects and crabs
The opening to a land snail's lung
items.why: Each word names a part that helps an animal get air. Knowing the right word helps you say exactly which part does the job.

items.p: Blood that stays inside tubes all the way round is called ____ circulation.
items.why: Closed circulation is found in people, earthworms and octopuses. Blood that leaves the tubes is open circulation.

items.p: An ant manages with open blood. What is the reason?
opts: Her air tubes bring the oxygen, not her blood
She is too big for closed blood
items.why: In an insect the air tubes take oxygen straight to the cells. The blood does not have to carry it fast, so a simple heart and open blood are enough.

items.p: Which one has open blood, and is the odd one out? Earthworm, octopus, person, crab.
items.a: Crab, because the others have closed blood.
items.why: Earthworms, octopuses and people all keep their blood in tubes. A crab's haemolymph leaves the tubes and soaks round her organs.

items.p: In the Wobbly Walk game, an ant needed 18 flips and a crab needed 70. About how many times as many flips did the crab need? Give the nearest whole number.
items.why: 70 divided by 18 is about 3.9, so about 4. The crab's trip was only 2 times as long as the ant's, but the crab needed about 4 times as many flips.

items.p: Sort each place by where the gas exchange happens.
cats: On the outside of the body
items: On the outside of the body
On the outside of the body
On the outside of the body
items.why: Thin animals use their outer skin. Thicker animals fold the surface inside, as gills, tubes or book lungs, so it reaches deeper while staying protected.

items.p: Put these eight-cube shapes in order, from the fewest faces touching the air to the most.
a: A flat layer 2 cubes by 4 cubes
items.why: The faces that touch other cubes are hidden. A solid block hides the most (24 faces show). A flat layer shows 28. A line shows 34. Spread apart, all 48 faces show.

items.p: Explain why a gill is feathery and not a smooth lump.
items.a: More of a feathery gill touches the water, so more oxygen can drift in. A lump has most of its inside far from the water.
items.why: A strong answer says that a feathery shape has more surface, and says that more surface means faster gas exchange.

items.p: In Sugar Lumps, the crushed sugar vanished faster than the whole lump. Write what this shows, and how a gill uses the same idea.
items.a: More of the crushed sugar touches the water, so it dissolves faster. A gill is spread into thin feathers, so more of it touches the water, and oxygen comes in faster.
items.why: A good answer links more surface touching the water to faster change in both sugar and gills.

items.p: Rukmini and Dev are talking about why earthworms come up on the road after rain.

views.who: Rukmini, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Rain floods their burrows and the air runs out. They come up to breathe.

views.who: Dev, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Rain is their one chance to cross open ground without drying out. They come up to travel.

items.ask: Whose idea do you agree with more? What could you look for to find out?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and suggests a test, such as checking whether worms also surface in light rain when the soil is not flooded.
items.why: Scientists still argue about this. Both ideas have some evidence. A good test would separate the two ideas.

items.p: Draw a spider from below. Show a book lung as a stack of thin plates, and label the air opening.
items.a: A spider's belly with a small slit, and a stack of thin plates like pages inside it.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the plates as thin and stacked, so they have a lot of surface in a small space.

items.p: In Drop and Stir, the stirred glass was evenly coloured in seconds, but the still glass stayed patchy. What does this suggest about how a crab breathes?
opts: Moving water brings fresh water to the gills much faster than waiting
Crabs stir the water for fun
items.why: Still water spreads slowly, so the water next to the gills would soon run out of oxygen. A gill bailer keeps fresh water arriving.

items.p: A cube 6 centimetres wide has 216 cubic centimetres inside and 216 square centimetres outside. A cube 12 centimetres wide has 1,728 cubic centimetres inside and 864 square centimetres outside. How many cubic centimetres of inside are there for each square centimetre of outside in the 12 centimetre cube?
items.why: 1,728 divided by 864 is 2. The 6 centimetre cube has 1 for 1. Doubling the width doubles the inside for each bit of outside, so each bit of outside has twice as much to serve.

items.p: In a jelly, a colour takes 25 minutes to drift 1 millimetre. About how long would it take to drift 3 millimetres?
items.why: Three times as far takes about 3 times 3, which is 9, times as long. 9 times 25 is 225 minutes. A pick of 75 treats the drift as a straight run.

items.p: Suppose oxygen takes 1 minute to drift across 1 millimetre of tissue. About how many minutes would it take to drift across 10 millimetres?
items.why: Ten times as far takes about 10 times 10, which is 100, times as long. So 100 minutes. This is why a thick animal needs tubes or gills.

items.p: The blood of some crabs and spiders turns blue when it meets oxygen.
items.why: True. Their blood-like liquid carries oxygen using a copper-based substance, which is blue when it holds oxygen. Our blood uses iron, which is red.

items.p: A crab lives in warm water that holds little oxygen. Which change would help a bigger crab get enough?
opts: More gill surface and faster flow of water over it
items.why: More surface lets more oxygen drift in, and faster flow keeps fresh water arriving. Thicker skin would slow the drift down.

items.p: Match each animal to her trick for getting air.
pairs: Carries a bubble of air under her wing covers
Hangs at the top of the water to reach the air
Has gills inside her tail end
Swims up to fill her lung
items.why: Each animal lives where air is hard to reach, and each has found its own way. This shows that one problem can have many solutions.

items.p: Put these in order, from the earliest to the latest, in the story of oxygen.
a: Tiny bacteria in the sea make oxygen from sunlight
Oxygen builds up in the sea and the air
Animals appear that use the oxygen
A crab takes oxygen from water at her gills
items.why: Oxygen was made first by tiny living beings. It built up over a very long time. Animals came later and breathe it, so every breath depends on what others made.

items.p: Four times as long lets a drifting particle go only ____ as far.
items.why: Time goes with the square of the distance. So four times as long gives only twice as far.

items.p: Sort each fact by whether it is true of insect air tubes or crab gills.
items: Open to the air through small holes in the sides
Need water to flow over them
Sit in a chamber under the shell
Pass oxygen to blood, which carries it round
items.why: Insects breathe air through spiracles and tubes that end beside the cells. Crabs breathe water over gills, and their blood carries the oxygen onward.

items.p: Scientists disagree about why the giant insects of long ago died out. What is the honest thing to say?
opts: Several ideas fit the facts, and nobody knows for sure
items.why: Oxygen, flying hunters and body weight are all suggested. The fossils have gaps, so we cannot yet tell which, or which together, is right.

items.p: A land snail breathes with gills.
items.why: False. A land snail has a lung, a wet pocket under her shell, with a small opening called the breathing pore.

items.p: A friend says: 'The big jelly cube had a clear middle because the colour was too weak.' How could you test whether she is right?
items.a: Make the colour much stronger and test the same cube again. If the middle is still clear, the colour was not the reason. You could also cut a thinner piece, which should be coloured right through.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the strength of the colour and keeps everything else the same.

items.p: Explain why a lung is a clever way for a big animal to meet the air.
items.a: A lung folds a huge thin wet surface into a small space inside the body. Blood flows close to the air there, so oxygen drifts only a very short way, and the blood carries it round.
items.why: A strong answer says that it makes a lot of surface in a small space and brings blood and air close together.

items.p: Ananya and Imran are talking about giant insects that lived 300 million years ago.

views.who: Ananya, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: There was more oxygen in the air then. That is why insects could grow so big.

views.who: Imran, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Flying hunters appeared later and ate the big insects. The size was not about air.

items.ask: Whose idea do you agree with more? What evidence would change your mind?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and says what would change their mind, for example finding giants that lived when there was little oxygen.
items.why: Scientists are still arguing. Both ideas may be partly right. A good answer shows how to find evidence that could settle it.

items.p: Draw two bodies, one thin and one thick. Show with arrows how oxygen can reach the middle of each.
items.a: A thin body with short arrows through the skin, and a thick body with branching tubes, folds or a pump bringing the air inside.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that a thin body needs only short arrows from the outside, while a thick body needs tubes, folds or a pump to bring the air closer.

items.p: When is a still, weedy pond lowest in oxygen?
opts: In the middle of a sunny afternoon
items.why: In the dark, the plants cannot make oxygen, but plants and animals keep using it. By dawn the night's use has added up, and the oxygen is lowest.

quiz.p: A drifting particle needs a certain time to go a certain distance. Which statement is closest to the truth?
opts: Twice as far takes about four times as long
Twice as far takes twice as long
Distance makes no difference to the time
quiz.why: Drifting is a random wander, so each step forward can be undone. The time goes up with the square of the distance.

quiz.p: Which has more outside for each bit of inside?
quiz.why: Take a 1 centimetre cube and a 2 centimetre cube. The small one has 6 outside for 1 inside. The big one has 24 for 8, which is only 3 for each.

quiz.p: Which animal gets most of her air through her skin?
quiz.why: The earthworm is thin and has a wet skin. The crab uses gills, and the ant uses air tubes.

quiz.p: A caterpillar has a row of dark dots down her sides. What are they for?
opts: They let air in to her air tubes
quiz.why: They are spiracles. Air goes in through them and along the tubes to the parts that need it.

quiz.p: Why can a thin flatworm breathe through her skin alone, but a thick crab cannot?
opts: Oxygen drifts only a short way, so a thick body has a middle too far from the outside
quiz.why: Thin bodies keep every cell near the outside. A thick body needs gills, tubes or lungs to bring the outside closer.

quiz.p: A fish farmer sees fish gasping at dawn in a still, warm tank. What should she do first?
opts: Add air to the water, move it, and cool it
quiz.why: Still, warm water holds little oxygen, and the night has used it up. Moving and aerating the water brings oxygen back.

quiz.p: Whose blood carries most of her oxygen to her cells?
quiz.why: People carry oxygen in red blood. In ants and caterpillars, air tubes take the oxygen directly to the cells.

quiz.p: In open circulation, the blood-like liquid does what?
opts: It leaves the vessels and soaks round the organs
It stays inside tubes all the way round
quiz.why: Crabs, insects, spiders and snails have open circulation. Earthworms, octopuses and people have closed circulation.

quiz.p: In a fair test of dissolving sugar as a whole lump, in bits and as powder, what do you change?
opts: Only the shape of the sugar
The amount of water and the amount of sugar
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing. Everything else, such as the water and the amount of sugar, stays the same.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still argue about?
opts: Why the giant insects died out
quiz.why: Insects do have air tubes and crabs do have gills. Why the giants disappeared is not settled.

quiz.p: A spider has thin plates stacked inside her belly. What are they called?
quiz.why: A book lung is a stack of thin plates, like the pages of a book. Air flows between them and blood flows through them.

quiz.p: In Colour Cubes, a thin slice was coloured right through but the 2 centimetre cube kept a clear middle. Why?
opts: The middle of the big cube was too far from the edge for the colour to reach in that time
The slice was a different jelly
The big cube had no room
quiz.why: The colour crept in about the same few millimetres on each piece. The slice was thin enough to be reached from both sides, and the big cube was not.

applications: Fish and crab farms put in tide gates, fans and air pumps so the water keeps moving and carries enough oxygen.
Aquariums stay healthy when they are not crowded and not too warm, so the water keeps enough dissolved oxygen.
Gardeners use oil sprays on pests. A film of oil can block the air holes of small insects such as aphids.
Engineers copy the trick of folding a surface to make radiators, cooling coils and filters with a lot of area in a small space.
Doctors treat breathing problems by understanding how a thin, wet, folded surface works, as in lungs.

open_questions.q: Why did the giant insects of 300 million years ago die out?
open_questions.why_open: Fossils show that they lived, and scientists have several ideas, but no one can run the experiment on the whole ancient Earth.

open_questions.q: Why do earthworms come up when it rains?
open_questions.why_open: People have watched it for centuries. Careful tests have not yet separated breathing, travelling and danger from the rain.

open_questions.q: Did the first animals need much oxygen?
open_questions.why_open: Some living sponges can survive in water with very little oxygen. Scientists do not agree on whether oxygen rose before animals appeared, or after.

open_questions.q: Why do some insects open their air holes only now and then, and keep them shut in between?
open_questions.why_open: The pattern is clear in some beetles, but scientists still argue about whether it saves water, helps in the low-oxygen air of burrows, or does something else.

open_questions.q: When a crab gasps in water that has little air, does she feel something like we do when we are short of breath?
open_questions.why_open: A crab cannot tell us. Scientists look at what she does, and many now think crabs may feel pain, but no one can be sure what it is like.

maths.problem: In Ring or Core, the red ring had 4, 12, 20 and 28 cells in squares 2, 4, 6 and 8 cells wide. What pattern do the ring numbers follow? Use it to find the ring for a square 10 cells wide and 12 cells wide.
maths.answer: Each ring is 8 more than the last. A 10 wide square has 36 ring cells. A 12 wide square has 44.
maths.explain: 4 plus 8 is 12, 12 plus 8 is 20, and 20 plus 8 is 28. Going on, 28 plus 8 is 36, and 36 plus 8 is 44. You could also use the rule: 4 times the width, take away 4.
maths.context: In Ring or Core, you draw squares and count the edge cells and the middle cells.
maths.why_maths: A pattern lets you work out the ring of a much bigger body without drawing it.

maths.problem: In Colour Cubes, the colour crept 2 millimetres into the jelly in 10 minutes. If it keeps to the same rule, about how long to creep 4 millimetres, and how long to creep 6 millimetres?
maths.answer: About 40 minutes for 4 millimetres, and about 90 minutes for 6 millimetres.
maths.explain: 4 millimetres is twice as far, so about 2 times 2, which is 4, times as long: 40 minutes. 6 millimetres is three times as far, so about 3 times 3, which is 9, times as long: 90 minutes.
maths.context: In Colour Cubes, you see colour creep into jelly more and more slowly.
maths.why_maths: A rule that links distance to time lets you predict how long a colour or a bit of oxygen takes to travel, before you wait for it.

maths.problem: A cube 1 centimetre wide has 6 square centimetres of outside, a cube 2 centimetres wide has 24, and a cube 3 centimetres wide has 54. How many times bigger is the outside of the 3 centimetre cube than the 1 centimetre cube? How many times bigger is its inside, if the 1 centimetre cube holds 1 cubic centimetre and the 3 centimetre cube holds 27?
maths.answer: Its outside is 9 times bigger and its inside is 27 times bigger.
maths.explain: 54 divided by 6 is 9. 27 divided by 1 is 27. The inside grows faster than the outside, so each bit of inside is further from the outside in the bigger cube.
maths.context: You have counted faces of cubes of different sizes.
maths.why_maths: Comparing how fast the outside and the inside grow shows why a bigger animal needs more help to get oxygen to the middle of their body.

maths.problem: Zoya played Wobbly Walk. For the ant she needed 14, 22 and 19 flips. For the crab she needed 61, 88 and 52. Find the average for each. About how many times as many flips did the crab need?
maths.answer: Ant: 55 divided by 3 is about 18 flips. Crab: 201 divided by 3 is 67 flips. The crab needed about 4 times as many.
maths.explain: 14 plus 22 plus 19 is 55. 55 divided by 3 is about 18. 61 plus 88 plus 52 is 201. 201 divided by 3 is 67. 67 divided by 18 is about 4.
maths.context: In Wobbly Walk, you flip a coin to move a token towards the middle of a body.
maths.why_maths: An average smooths out the luck of any single try, so you can compare the bodies fairly.

maths.problem: In Wobbly Walk, the token goes in on heads and back on tails. If you flip a fair coin 100 times, about how many heads and how many tails will you get? Where will the token be, on average, and why does it take so long to reach the middle?
maths.answer: About 50 heads and 50 tails. The steps in and out cancel, so the token ends up near where it started. It only reaches the middle when chance happens to give a run of heads.
maths.explain: A fair coin gives heads about half the time. About half of the steps go in and half go back. Nothing pushes the token in one direction, so it wanders, and wandering covers a long distance very slowly.
maths.context: In Wobbly Walk, a coin decides every step of an oxygen particle's wander.
maths.why_maths: Chance helps explain why drifting is slow. The wander makes no progress unless a run of heads happens by luck.

maths.problem: Water holds about 30 times less oxygen than air. A crab needs the oxygen in 2 litres of air every hour. About how many litres of water must pass over her gills in an hour? In 10 hours?
maths.answer: About 60 litres in an hour. About 600 litres in 10 hours.
maths.explain: She needs 30 times as much water, because it holds 30 times less oxygen. 2 times 30 is 60 litres. In 10 hours that is 10 times 60, which is 600 litres.
maths.context: You have learned that water holds much less oxygen than air.
maths.why_maths: A ratio shows how much more water than air an animal with gills must move, which is why gills need a bailer or a current.

maths.problem: A still pond holds 9 milligrams of oxygen in a litre of water at 20 degrees. At 30 degrees it holds 7.5 milligrams in a litre. How many milligrams less does it hold when warm? Is that more than one-tenth less, or less than one-tenth less?
maths.answer: 1.5 milligrams less. One-tenth of 9 is 0.9, so it is more than one-tenth less.
maths.explain: 9 take away 7.5 is 1.5. One-tenth of 9 is 0.9, and 1.5 is bigger than 0.9. So warm water holds noticeably less, about one-sixth less.
maths.context: You learned that warm water holds less oxygen than cold water.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a drop with a fraction of the starting amount shows how serious a small warming can be for a crab or fish.

how_we_found_out.story: About 330 BCE, the Greek thinker Aristotle taught that animals breathe to cool the heat of the heart. He called animals such as insects 'bloodless'. For nearly two thousand years, people repeated this. Nobody could say how a caterpillar with no lungs got air. In 1669 an Italian doctor, Marcello Malpighi, studied silkworms through an early microscope. He saw a row of tiny holes down each side. Inside, thin pale tubes ran from each hole and branched again and again into finer threads. Malpighi had found the silkworm's air tubes. Air does not travel in blood here. It goes straight to the parts that need it. Later, Antoine Lavoisier showed in the 1770s and 1780s that breathing uses up part of the air, which is oxygen, in a slow burning that warms the body. In 1919 the Danish scientist August Krogh measured how fast gases drift through animal bodies, and showed that drifting works well over short distances.
how_we_found_out.who: Marcello Malpighi, an Italian doctor (1628 to 1694)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Aristotle thought breathing cools the heart, and that insects were 'bloodless' animals. Malpighi's microscope showed that insects have air tubes reaching every part, and later work showed that every cell uses oxygen.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. Colour Cubes is the key test, so it was worked out carefully. Agar jelly set with 2 teaspoons of powder in 500 millilitres of water holds a cut cube, and food colour moves in about 2 to 3 millimetres in 40 minutes and about 1 to 2 millimetres in 10 minutes. The exact numbers will vary, and the steps say to write what you see. If the colour is too pale, add more food colour. If a cube is coloured right through, cut the next one earlier. Wobbly Walk was run many times on a computer: with a coin, the average number of flips is about 6 for a 2-square body, 20 for 4 squares and 72 for 8 squares, and about 14 flips for 8 squares with the pump. Sugar cube dissolving times depend on the water temperature, so the steps use the same glass and water for every test. Facts to check before this unit goes live: that air holds about 30 times more oxygen than the same amount of water, that the coconut crab lives on the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, that Meganeura wings were about 65 to 70 centimetres across, that Krogh's 1919 paper made the diffusion point, that the 2003 X-ray study of beetles is correctly described, and that the Marine Biodiversity Museum in Kochi is open to visitors. Colour Cubes takes about 90 minutes from start to finish, because the jelly must set and the colour needs 40 minutes, but only about 50 minutes are hands-on, and the waiting time suits Ring or Core.
